bio.en: Sriram Krishnan and Aarthi Ramamurthy are the hosts of The Aarthi and Sriram Show; Sriram is a former Microsoft/Twitter exec and a16z partner (later a senior White House AI advisor), and Aarthi is a former Netflix, Spotify, and Microsoft product leader and founder of Latent.
bio.zh: Sriram Krishnan 与 Aarthi Ramamurthy 是《The Aarthi and Sriram Show》的主持人：Sriram 曾任 Microsoft/Twitter 高管与 a16z 合伙人（后任白宫高级 AI 顾问），Aarthi 则是前 Netflix、Spotify、Microsoft 产品领导者，也是 Latent 的创始人。

summary.en: Sriram and Aarthi share lessons from building, operating, and investing across tech, including a pointed critique of the Jobs-to-be-Done framework and what they'd use instead. They discuss how to pick roles, the value of learning in public, and the behind-the-scenes of getting famously hard-to-book guests on their show. The conversation is wide-ranging, funny, and full of practitioner wisdom on careers and product.
summary.zh: Sriram 与 Aarthi 分享了横跨科技圈打造、运营与投资的经验，包括对“待办任务（Jobs-to-be-Done）”框架的尖锐批评，以及他们会用什么来取代它。他们讨论了如何选择职位、公开学习的价值，以及把那些出了名难约的嘉宾请上节目的幕后故事。对话涉猎广泛、妙趣横生，充满了关于职业与产品的实践者智慧。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: I hate Jobs-to-be-Done, I think it is a terrible framework, I think no successful company has ever been built on top of JTBD and if you pick JTBD, you're probably doomed and I'll give you an example. When you sign up for Instagram right now, when you sign up for Facebook for many, many years, Facebook knew that it needed to get you to 10 friends in 14 days. If you got your 10 friends in 14 days, you were probably going to use Facebook. So it'd be like, "Well, we're going to throw every tool we have at our disposal to get you to 10 friends and 14 days." (00:00:23): So if you signed up for Facebook for many, many years, you'll get this little thing called People You May Know. Then you'll have this person who just signed up for Facebook, you go, "Why I'm seeing this person?" It's not because you need a friend, because they need a friend. So what Facebook did was it made your experience slightly worse to make that person's experience slightly better. This was performing no job for you, it was trying to perform a job for them.
turns.zh: 我讨厌"待办任务"（Jobs-to-be-Done）这个框架，我认为它糟糕透顶。没有任何成功的公司是基于JTBD框架建立起来的，如果你选择JTBD，恐怕注定要失败。我来举个例子。现在注册Instagram，或者多年前注册Facebook时，Facebook深知必须在14天内帮你加满10个好友。只要你成功在14天内加满10个好友，就很可能继续使用Facebook。所以Facebook会动用一切手段，强行让你在14天内加满10个好友。（00:00:23）如果你注册Facebook多年，就会收到"你可能认识的人"这个功能。然后你会看到刚注册的用户，心里会想："为什么我会看到这个人？"这不是因为你需要朋友，而是因为对方需要朋友。所以Facebook这么做，是在降低你的体验感来提升对方的体验感。这根本不是在为你服务，而是为了他们自己。

(00:06:39): In Elon's case actually, what wound up happening was a few years ago, he DMed me out of the blue. At the time, I was working at Twitter and I think he saw something I'd written and wanted something from the company and I think he went through the org chart and he DMed me. And I was like, "Well, I'd love to help you," and he sent me his phone number. And I called him and I was like, "Is this [inaudible 00:07:00] and we had a conversation and we built up a relationship after that. This was when Clubhouse first came on the scene and I was like, "Well, who do we get on?" and Elon hadn't done a lot of press appearances, I think he's done a lot more since then obviously, and I texted him and he was like, "I'm game," and the rest is history.

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, all good questions here. I think growth strategy, that's a great way to acquire people right at the top of the funnel. Once you've done this a few times, you kind of see everything as a funnel and you're like, "Well, are you retaining people? Are you not? Is it top of the funnel impressions or do they stick around?" So I think having people like Marc Andreessen and people like Naval and they were not doing this out of any... they were really, really interested. I will say, Clubhouse, I feel like they get this unfair attention and criticism. It's a what, three-year-old startup?
turns.zh: 是啊，这些问题都很不错。我认为增长策略确实是获取用户的绝佳方式，尤其是在用户获取漏斗的顶端。经过多次实践后，你会把所有事情都视为漏斗效应，然后思考：用户留存率如何？是否达标？是漏斗顶端的曝光量不足，还是用户留存时间不够？所以邀请像马克·安德森和纳维尔这样的人加入确实很明智。他们并非为了投机而来，他们是真心热爱这项技术。当马克邀请我们加入时，他就直言：“看看这个产品……这甚至是在a16z投资之前的事。他就说：‘这个产品太棒了，这些人做得很棒，这就是未来，太了不起了。’所以这给了他们一个平台，让他们能畅谈和直播社交音频，效果非常好。说实话，Clubhouse确实受到了不公正的批评和指责。它才成立三年啊！

Is this a pandemic fad versus not?" I don't know, it's a product at the end of the day and you're going to have to find product market fit and I think they'll figure it out.
turns.zh: 我自己也创过两家公司。第二家公司成立三年时，我们还在摸索方向。所以我觉得创业者需要时间喘息，理清思路。我看好Clubhouse，相信他们会找到出路的。保罗和罗汉都是优秀的创业者。他们在社交领域深耕十多年了，一定能找到方向。我知道人们会说：‘他们在疫情期间很火，但这只是疫情期间的潮流？’我不确定，但归根结底这是一个产品，你必须找到产品与市场的契合点，我相信他们会做到的。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah. The broader question of how do social products acquire the users is super interesting. One of my favorite pieces written on this is Eugene Wei's Status as a Service. Eugene should absolutely be on your podcast someday. It's a 10,000 word piece, which is amazing and highly suggest people read it. But one of the key takeaways from that piece is the idea that when you have a new network, think of it as a new country, you want the high status people and high status mean they're interesting, people want to be where they are in some shape or form because they have money, they're smart, they're cool, they're good-looking, whatever it may be and you want to get them onto your network. And there's exactly an interesting corollary that they're often underserved by other existing platforms. And because if they're already well-served, they wouldn't want to move to you. (00:11:43): And Eugene doesn't talk about it, but if I look at say the history of all the three, four large social media companies, you've seen this pattern. For example, they've often each had a breakout set of stars who are unique to the platform. For example, if you look at say Snapchat, you had folks like Kylie Jenner who really broke out first. If you look at Instagram, I would think The Rock, Cristiano Ronaldo, a lot of others are organic to Instagram. But let's say you get to TikTok. One of the things you'll see is a lot of the folks from the Instagram world rarely move to TikTok and there's a couple of reasons. One, they didn't really need to because they were already popular on some of these other existing platforms, but two, TikTok actually took advantage of a different set of skillsets. People who are really good on video, people who could dance, be funny. And so you saw the rise of Charli D'Amelio and Addison and so many others who are different. (00:12:31): So every single time, I think you need to go after a set of people who are high status who are also underserved. So coming back to Clubhouse, I think one of the interesting things is I think these celebrities are super interesting, but what is more interesting for me is all the homegrown folks. I actually consider us as a part of that, we would not be here doing the show if it wasn't for Clubhouse. There are many folks who had that original launch using the platform, so I think for folks here who are thinking about social platforms, it's interesting about okay, you need interesting people from elsewhere, but you also need homegrown talent. And by the way, you are a perfect example of this phenomenon because you are Substack's homegrown talent and I think you bring a lot of value to Substack. And there are a lot of people with huge newsletters, et cetera, but I think your rise and your popularity is so tied to Substack now and that's actually a great example of all of this.
turns.zh:
是啊。我觉得社交产品如何获取用户这个更宏观的问题非常有趣。我最喜欢的一篇关于这个主题的文章是尤金·韦（Eugene Wei）的《地位即服务》（Status as a Service）。你真应该邀请尤金上你的播客聊聊。这篇文章长达1万字，非常精彩，强烈推荐大家读一读。但文章的一个关键观点是，当你推出一个新社交网络时，可以把它想象成一个新国家。你需要吸引那些地位高的人——所谓地位高的人，通常意味着他们很有趣，人们想加入他们的原因可能是他们有钱、聪明、酷、有魅力等等。而这些人在现有平台上往往得不到充分服务，正因为如此，他们才会愿意迁移到你的平台上。

（00:11:43）尤金没有深入探讨，但回顾过去三四家大型社交媒体公司的历史，我们能发现类似的模式。比如，他们各自都有一批在平台上独树一帜的明星。以Snapchat为例，凯莉·詹娜（Kylie Jenner）最早在这里崭露头角。再看Instagram，巨石强森（The Rock）、克里斯蒂亚诺·罗纳尔多（Cristiano Ronaldo）等明星也都是平台的原生用户。但到了TikTok，你会发现很多Instagram上的用户很少迁移过去，原因有二：一是他们在其他平台已经很受欢迎，不需要转战；二是TikTok充分利用了不同技能组的人才，比如擅长视频制作、跳舞、搞笑的人。正因如此，查莉·达梅利奥（Charli D'Amelio）、艾迪森（Addison）等新晋网红才得以崛起。

（00:12:31）每次成功的社交产品，都需要吸引既有高地位又被现有平台忽视的用户群体。回到Clubhouse，我觉得这些名人固然很有趣，但更让我感兴趣的是平台上本土培养的用户。比如我们Substack就是平台的原生人才，如果没有Clubhouse，我们就不会在这里做节目。许多人最初使用Clubhouse时就抓住了这个机会。因此，对于关注社交平台的人来说，关键在于吸引其他平台的优质用户，同时也要重视本土人才的发展。顺便说一句，你就是这个现象的完美例子——你作为Substack的本土人才，为Substack带来了巨大价值。虽然Substack上有很多订阅量巨大的新闻简报等内容，但你的成功和受欢迎程度与Substack紧密相连，这正是上述观点的绝佳例证。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It reminds me, the founder of Musical.ly who turned into TikTok has a great story. I think you've heard his talk about this, how the way he thought about it is there's all these successful people on Instagram, that's Europe, and the people you can convince to come to America are not the kings of Europe, but they're the peasants that are like, "Oh, we have a new opportunity to rise and become a king or a queen." And so those are the people you pull in, the people not doing well on another platform that want to do well versus the people already killing it.
turns.zh: 是啊。这让我想起TikTok的前身Musical.ly的创始人，他的故事很精彩。我相信你听过他对此的分享。他认为Instagram上有很多成功人士，但在欧洲市场，而那些能被说服来美国的人并非欧洲的王者，而是愿意抓住新机遇、成为新王者的平民。因此，吸引这些在其他平台上表现不佳、但渴望成功的人才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah, [inaudible 00:13:53].

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Lenny just called himself the king of Substack right there.
turns.zh: 莱尼刚刚在那儿自称是Substack之王。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yes, I know. You're the king, you're the king of Americas.
turns.zh: 是啊，我知道。你就是国王，你是美国的国王。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: I'm just trying to give you clippable moments on video.
turns.zh: 我只是想在视频里给你一些能被剪辑成片段的精彩瞬间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did just find out that I think I have the fourth-largest Substack newsletter on all of Substack which is ridiculous-
turns.zh: 我刚发现，我觉得我在Substack上订阅的新闻简报规模是全平台第四大，这太不可思议了——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: That's amazing, wow. That's amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了，哇。太棒了。

turns.en: Their recent number.

turns.en: Yeah. Number three, number two, number one, Lenny is coming after you, better watch out.

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Take them out.
turns.zh: 把他们干掉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. They're up there. So you mentioned the chat with Elon and how you're very tech positive and I think that's something that you two are at the forefront of, is this trend, I don't know if it's called techno-optimism or maybe there's another term for it and I'd love to hear just like why? Because I know that's important to you too, why that's important to you and just what is this movement of techno-optimism-
turns.zh: 是啊。他们在上面。所以你提到了和埃隆的聊天，以及你对科技非常乐观。我觉得你们俩是这一趋势的先锋，我不知道这是否被称为技术乐观主义，或者可能有其他术语，我很想听听原因？因为我知道这对你也很重要，为什么这对你很重要，以及技术乐观主义这一运动到底是什么？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Let me take a small stab at it. Look, I think it's also very personal to our context and our upbringing. For us, Sriram and I came from a fairly middle class family in India, this city in India that most people here won't probably know. And we grew up really liking computers but didn't have access to a computer for a longest time. In both our cases, our parents bought us our first computers after saving money for it and it was a hard thing. And when we eventually got onto it and started learning to write code, we met each other online. We're dating ourselves now, but we met on Yahoo Messenger back in the day and we worked on this nerdy coding project, that's how we connected. So technology and computers have given us everything. (00:15:19): Our first jobs were at Microsoft, we built developer tools and platforms. If you were in our shoes, you would feel the same way too. Tech has given us so much. And so for us to come here all the way from India, through multiple cities, we lived in Seattle and then here, the Bay Area, I've started tech companies, it is a bit frustrating to see the other viewpoint because you can see how much it has uplifted people, careers, lives, but also just from what we've been able to work on, what we've seen our friends work on and ship and put out there, it has dramatically moved the needle. And so for us, we are the living testament of tech actually helping us and help us do better, so I don't even see the other viewpoint from like, why wouldn't you be optimistic about technology? I don't get it.
turns.zh: 让我简单说一下。看，我认为这也与我们的背景和成长环境密切相关。对于我们来说，斯里拉姆和我来自印度的一个中产阶级家庭，这个城市可能很多人都不知道。我们从小就喜欢电脑，但很长时间都用不上电脑。我们俩都是父母存钱后给我们买了第一台电脑，这很不容易。当我们最终接触到电脑并开始学习编程时，我们在网上认识了彼此。我们现在可以自嘲是网恋对象，但当时我们是在雅虎通上认识的，然后一起做了一个技术宅的编程项目，就是这样建立了联系。所以科技和电脑给了我们一切。（00:15:19）我们的第一份工作是在微软，开发开发者工具和平台。如果你处在我们的位置，你也会有同样的感受。科技给了我们太多。然后我们从印度一路走来，经过多个城市，住在西雅图，再到湾区，我创办了科技公司。看到另一种观点确实有点令人沮丧，因为你能看到科技如何提升了人们的地位、职业生涯和生活，但从我们参与的项目、朋友们的成果来看，它确实带来了巨大的改变。对我们来说，我们就是科技帮助我们成功的活生生的例子，所以我甚至不理解为什么有人不乐观看待科技？我真不明白。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah. I think the personal part was really core. I think there's generally two schools of thought. One school of thought, I would broadly write up as things are getting worse, technology is making things worse and we should all do less, build less. And then the other school of thought, which I think I subscribe to, is technology is not perfect, the impact technology is definitely uneven, but pretty much most of the good things in the world over the last 100, 200 years are responsible for it. And we can have a whole long discussion about the evidence why and we have lots of very fancy sounding intellectual theories as to why, but at the heart of it is what Aarthi said, if it wasn't for tech, we wouldn't be here, we wouldn't be doing this. (00:16:45): I suspect a lot of folks who are listening to this wouldn't be able to listen to it, wouldn't have the opportunities they have or have the opportunities we have. It is a great level up. My dad pretty much had the same job for his entire life, essentially from age 25 till the time he retired and there was really no easy path out for him. And I imagine like, "Hey, if he was born 40 years later and he had a laptop and an internet connection and could get on GitHub, here are opportunities that would be just impossible, even 30, 40 years ago and that's all from technology." So I think that's at the heart of it, it's the best thing we have of getting ahead.
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为个人层面的影响至关重要。大体上，有两种观点流派。一种观点认为情况正在恶化，科技让问题雪上加霜，所以我们应该减少生产、减少建设。而另一种观点——我个人认同——是科技虽不完美，其影响确实不均衡，但过去一百年、两百年间，世界上大多数好事都得益于科技。我们可以长篇大论地探讨其中的证据，人们也提出了许多高深莫测的理论来解释其中的因果关系，但归根结底，正如阿尔提所说，如果没有科技，我们就不会站在这里参与这场对话。（00:16:45）我相信许多听众都无法收听这期节目，如果没有科技，他们根本没有机会获得现有的机遇。科技确实带来了巨大的进步。我父亲几乎一辈子从事同一项工作，自25岁起直到退休，几乎没有其他出路。我能想象，如果他出生在40年后，拥有笔记本电脑和互联网连接，能登录GitHub，那些在三四十年前看来不可思议的机会对他而言都将触手可及，这一切都源自科技。所以我认为这才是关键所在，科技是我们进步的最佳助力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a refreshing perspective on tech. In traditional media, all you ever hear about is all the problems that tech is causing and all the dangers and how we're all screwed. And so it's like you almost forget that there could be really positive stories about what's happening with tech and it feels like there's a small number of people that are doing this at scale and-
turns.zh: 这真是对科技的一种令人耳目一新的看法。在传统媒体中，人们听到的全是科技带来的种种问题、各种危险，仿佛我们都深陷其中。人们几乎忘记了，科技也能带来积极的变化。令人欣慰的是，确实有一些人在大规模践行这种理念——

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Oh, yeah. I'll give you one small example. You made a joke about kings from Europe, et cetera. If we just go back 100 years, the piece of hardware that a king or a royalty would use or a rich person would use would be so different from what a peasant would use, but you know what? I suspect the phone that you and I have is probably the same phone that... actually I know it's the same phone that Elon Musk uses, the richest person in the world. I know a lot of folks in India who have very high end Android device, they have access to the same internet. You go to google.com, google.com doesn't know your net worth, it gives you the same results. Chat GPT doesn't know how rich you are. It may not like you, but it doesn't know how rich you are. If you just think of all these constructs, they're were just impossible technology. But anyway, that's a whole other conversation.
turns.zh: 哦，对啊。我举个小例子。你开玩笑说欧洲国王之类的。如果回溯到一百年前，国王、皇室成员或富人使用的硬件设备与农民使用的相比简直天差地别。但你知道吗？我敢打赌，你我用的手机很可能和世界首富埃隆·马斯克用的手机是一样的。我认识很多印度人，他们用着高端安卓设备，访问的互联网资源也一样。访问谷歌时，谷歌不会识别你的财富状况，提供的搜索结果一视同仁。ChatGPT也不知道你有多富有。它可能不喜欢你，但绝不会判断你的财富水平。若仔细想想，这些科技成果在过去简直不可思议。不过这又是一个复杂的话题了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love that the richest people have the same phone as me and nothing they can do about it. Something else you two are really good at is building a network, building community, building personal brands. I know a lot of people listening are either often told, "You need to build a audience online, you build a brand, you got to build a network," and all these things. So I guess I'd love to know just what advice do you give people that come to you and like, "Hey, I want to build a personal brand, I want to build the network"? Just how to go about doing that, what's worked well for you two?
turns.zh: 是啊，我很欣赏最富有的人和我用的手机一样，却对此无能为力。你们两位还非常擅长建立人脉、社区和个人品牌。我知道很多听众常被告知“你需要在网上积累受众、打造品牌、建立人脉”之类的话。所以我想知道，你们会给那些来找你们的人什么建议？比如，“嘿，我想打造个人品牌，建立人脉”，该怎么做呢？对你们俩来说哪些方法有效？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Sriram has way more structured thoughts on this and honestly, he's way better at this than I've ever been. He's basically slowly corrupted me and brought me to the dark side. But what I have come to believe and this differs from what I used to believe is especially if you're working in a big company, you are one of the many thousands of employees in there. Generally what you get told is, "Hey, just ship really good products, put your head down, go to work. The products will speak for themselves. That's just how it's going to work. Don't do this whole personal branding and all of that stuff. It's such a distraction," and that's generally what you're told. (00:19:34): Most of my career I was like, "Yeah, of course that makes sense, that's kind of what you do." But I've come to realize that that is just not true and this might be a controversial opinion, but you have to get out there and build your own brand. You have to figure out what you stand for, what your core values are, what you believe in, what you think you want to do, what your next career trajectory is going to look like. All of that is just up to you. It's not up to the company to figure it out for you, it's not up to anybody else, it's just up to you. (00:20:05): And I think building a personal brand is looked down upon so much that people think of it as a dirty word. It's like, "No, you can't do that." "Oh, look at this person who's branding themselves," kind of thing. But I almost see it as what distinguishes you from everybody else and that is not so much saying something that you're not good at or touting yourself more, it's really about highlighting, "I'm really good at this thing and I want to talk about this thing and I want to do videos about it or write about it or tweet about it." Whatever is your forum, you have to put yourself out there.
turns.zh: 斯里拉姆对此有更系统的见解，说实话，他在这方面比我强多了。他基本上慢慢把我带坏了，把我带向了黑暗面。但我现在逐渐意识到——这和我过去的想法有所不同——尤其是在大公司工作时，你只是成千上万名员工中的一员。通常公司会对你说："嘿，只要交出优质产品，埋头工作，产品会自己说话的。事情就是这样。别搞什么个人品牌建设之类的玩意儿，那纯粹是分心之举。"这就是他们常说的。（00:19:34）我职业生涯的大部分时间都觉得，"是啊，这说得通啊，这就是该做的。"但我现在意识到，这根本就不是事实。这或许是个有争议的观点，但你必须走出去，打造自己的品牌。你得弄清楚自己的立场、核心价值观、信仰、职业规划，以及未来的发展方向。这些都取决于你自己，而不是公司，也不是其他人。（00:20:05）我觉得打造个人品牌这件事被看得太低了，人们甚至把它视为贬义词。比如："不行，你不能这么做。"或者"看看那个人在营销自己"之类的。但我认为这恰恰能让你在人群中脱颖而出。这不是在掩饰自己不擅长的地方，也不是在自我吹嘘，而是要突出自己的专长："我真的很擅长这个领域，我想谈论它，制作视频、写文章、发推特。"无论用何种平台，你都得把自己推向公众视野。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: I mean this is probably one of the most important things that somebody can do and I spent... no, we spent years slowly climbing the corporate ranks. We were junior product managers, IC product managers, senior product managers, slowly climbed the ranks and ran teams, et cetera. And I spent years just thinking that all I need to do is put my head down, do my job really well and that was it. But then I looked around and I suspect a lot of listeners here probably have the same feeling that some sort of people were getting way more opportunities, some sort of people are way farther ahead even though I was mostly sure that somebody else was doing a better job and I was trying to understand why. And I think building a network, which I'll try and define because I think a lot of people have assumption of what it is, is at the heart of this. So building a network is very simply having relationships with human beings. And let's start off by saying first of all, these have to be authentic, genuine relationships. (00:21:29): One thing, it drives me crazy when somebody will come and say, "I'm here to network." I'm like, "I don't know what that word means." So all you're trying to do is have authentic, genuine relationship with people and expecting nothing in return, so that's great. And then people are like, "Oh, well that's awesome, but I'm a senior... for example, I was a senior PM at Microsoft for a bunch of time and then kind of similar at Facebook for a bunch of time, you're like, "Well, what does it mean? I'm here, I'm going to my meetings, I'm doing my day, its only so many hours." I'll be like, "Well, let's start off with go and meet every single peer that you have you don't directly meet with. Go get coffee with them and ask them, 'Hey.' Have no agenda. Just ask them what's going on in their life, who are they, what their life story is and then who are a couple of interesting people that you should meet with? Go talk to your manager and go talk to their peers." (00:22:14): Super important, by the way, your manager, peer relations are super important. Go have a coffee with them and they'd be like, "Great, I'm love to meet this person." Then when I joined at Facebook, I was notorious for being the person who sent a cold email to every single Facebook leader. And I'd be like, "Hey, I'm new here, I want to meet. Let's grab coffee," and everybody will say as everyone is a new person and always asking the same thing, which I'll be like, I show up, I'll tell them my story, I'll ask for their story. I'll be like, "What are you folks focused on? How can I help?" Again, no expectation of anything in return. And then I'll be like, "Who else should I talk to?" (00:22:42): You do this, you do two coffees a week and literally just ask me two hours a week, everyone has two hours a week, it'll start compounding over overtime and time. And then as the years go by, you keep in touch with the people you used to work with you, these folks will go to other places, five years, six years go by, you start in your mid-20s or late 20s and you know hundreds of people all over. And the important thing about this is that it is a resource in so many different places. For example, one, if you ever need help, you're trying to look for a new role or you're trying to be like, "Hey, I want to hire this person, who knows something about this person?" or, "I want a new role. Who's looking for something?" that network becomes your key resource. (00:23:21): Now what I think a lot of people don't do, it's just simple things. Number one is often people just have a great meeting with a peer and then they will never ever follow up. I'm sure a lot of us have the amazing first introduction email they never followed up, don't do that. I try and make it a point to make sure I always meet them once a year, once every six months. I'll just leave a note, "Hey, what's up?" And the other key part is expecting nothing in return. And generally people are very good at reading other people and if you go and being like, "Hey, I just want to meet you because I want a job or I'm here to network," whatever that means, they don't want to meet you. Just go and be very curious about who they are and try and help them. And you'll be surprised wherever you start, within a year, two years, you'll know hundreds of people who you can tap into, so I think that is super powerful. That's just building relationships. (00:24:05): The other part is brand building. Both Aarthi and I at different points in our career have gotten feedback in our job saying, "Oh, with Sriram and Aarthi, it's brand build too much, et cetera." I have learned that that is terrible feedback and to totally ignore that and if anybody hears anything like that, just totally ignore that. The things that work well for me and a lot of others is putting yourself out there and that can be anything. That can be like you make a presentation internally, you write tweets, you're prolific on GitHub, you make a YouTube video, it doesn't really matter, but put yourself out there because the internet rewards people being out there. And what happens when you put yourself out there? It's a Bat-Signal. It's telling people that, "Hey, I'm here, this is my body of work," and you know what the internet does? It'll send amazing people to you. (00:24:45): You'd be amazed how often somebody just have a random great Twitter thread with no followers and somebody super interesting will email them and that leads to amazing things happening, it encourages serendipity. So over the years, I wish I had listened less to people who said I should not do this and listened more to the people who said I should do this more.
turns.zh:
我想，这或许是人们能做的最重要的事之一。我花了……不，我们花了多年时间慢慢攀升职场阶梯。我们曾是初级产品经理、IC产品经理、高级产品经理，一步步晋升并管理团队等。我曾多年深信只要埋头工作，出色完成任务就足够了。但后来我环顾四周，发现许多听众可能也有同感——有些人获得了更多机会，有些人遥遥领先，尽管我坚信其他人本可以做得更好。于是我开始思考，建立人脉关系（我会尽力定义这个概念，因为很多人对此存在误解）才是关键所在。简单来说，建立人脉就是与他人建立真诚的关系。首先，这些关系必须真诚无虚伪。（00:21:29）：有件事让我很头疼，有些人会说：“我是来拓展人脉的。”我会说：“我不知道这个词什么意思。”所以你只需与他人建立真诚的关系，不求回报，这就足够了。但人们又会说：“哦，这很棒，但我是个资深……比如，我在微软当了多年高级产品经理，在Facebook也待了很久。”我会说：“那又怎样？我参加会议，完成日常工作，每天时间有限。”我会说：“那就去拜访所有你不直接接触的同行。去和他们喝咖啡，主动问他们：‘嘿，你好吗？’不要带任何功利心，只是了解他们的生活、背景，以及他们认为值得认识的人是谁。去和你的经理及他的同事聊聊。” （00:22:14）：顺便说一句，和经理及同事建立良好关系至关重要。和他们喝咖啡时，他们会说：“太棒了，我很乐意见见那个人。” 我加入Facebook时，曾因给每位高管发送冷邮件而出名。我会说：“嘿，我新来的，想认识下大家。一起喝咖啡吧。” 大家会觉得又是一个新人总问同样问题的人，但我会露脸，讲述自己的故事，询问他们的经历，问：“你们在专注什么？我能帮上什么忙？” 同样，不求回报。然后我会问：“还有谁值得我去拜访？” （00:22:42）：坚持这样做，每周两次喝咖啡，每周只需投入两小时（每个人每周都有两小时空闲时间），随着时间推移，效果会逐渐显现。几年后，你会和曾经共事过的人保持联系，他们离职后五六年，你已结识了数百位各界人士。关键在于，这份人脉资源能在多个场合发挥作用。比如，当你需要帮助、寻找新职位、想推荐某位候选人或寻找新机会时，这份人脉将成为你的核心资源。（00:23:21）：但我发现很多人做不到这些简单之事。第一，人们常因一次出色的会议而兴奋不已，却忽视了后续的跟进。会议只是开始，关键在于持续行动。
和某人初次见面后，他们往往再也不会跟进后续了。我相信很多人都有过那种令人惊叹的初次介绍邮件，却从未得到后续回应的经历。别这样做。我努力确保每年、每半年至少见他们一次。我只会留个简短的消息：“嘿，最近怎么样？”关键是别期待任何回报。通常人们很善于察言观色，如果你去见面时说：“嘿，我想见你是因为我在找工作/来拓展人脉”，无论你用什么说辞，他们都不想见你。你只需带着好奇心去了解对方，尽力帮助他们。无论从何处开始，一年、两年后，你都会认识数百个可以求助的人——这才是关键所在。这就是关系的建立。

（00:24:05）另一个关键是品牌建设。Aarthi和我在职业生涯的不同阶段都曾收到反馈：“和Sriram、Aarthi合作太注重品牌建设了之类的。” 我意识到这种反馈很糟糕，完全可以忽略。如果有人听到类似批评，直接无视即可。对我们和许多人有效的方法是主动展示自己，可以是内部演示、写推文、在GitHub上高产、制作YouTube视频——任何形式都可以。互联网会奖励那些主动表现的人。当你主动展示时，就像发射了蝙蝠信号，告诉人们：“嘿，我在这儿，这是我的成果。” 互联网会为你带来惊喜。

（00:24:45）你会惊讶于有多少例子：某个Twitter账号毫无粉丝，却能吸引感兴趣的人主动联系，进而引发奇妙的机缘。这些年来，我真希望自己少听那些劝阻的声音，多听那些支持的声音。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: I also think, Sriram keeps saying, "Expect nothing in return," I think the other way I see it is this is again an extension of optimism for us. Generally, we think people like to help each other out, that is just in their true nature. It's not meant to be transactional, it's not meant to be, "If I know them, they will somehow do something for me down the road," it's not that. Just the way we are all building communities and are a part of this broader community, the way we work is we all want to help each other and help them be successful. And if that is in your nature, it's hard to not feel like, "Yeah, of course I want to reach out to them. I want to see what I can do to help them. Maybe something good will happen, we'll collaborate on a project together," whatever. The core tenant being don't expect stuff in return, don't do it on a transactional basis, I think is really important.
turns.zh: 我也认为，正如Sriram一直强调的"别期待回报"，我理解的另一种方式是，这再次体现了我们对乐观精神的延续。通常，我们认为人们乐于互助，这正是他们的天性。这种互助不应建立在交易的基础上，不应想着，"只要我认识他们，他们日后就会为我做些什么"，而是应该本着共同建设社区、融入更广阔生态的初心，携手助力彼此成功。若你本性如此，就很难不产生"是的，我当然想主动联系他们。看看能帮上什么忙，或许会有好的合作"这样的想法。核心理念是别期待回报，别把互助当作交易，这一点至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What this reminds me of is Naval has this tweet that proved to be so true, which is don't network, instead create amazing things, create value, do good work and then people will want to network with you. And that's really stuck with me and it saves you from going to network events. Instead just go work hard, do awesome stuff and people are going to want to meet you.
turns.zh: 这让我想起Naval的那条推文，事实证明它极具洞察力：别去参加社交活动，而是专注创造价值、做好工作，这样人们自然会主动与你建立联系。这句话让我深有共鸣，也省去了参加社交活动的麻烦。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: I mean you will not believe the number of times I've shown up to some meetup or some founder thing or something and then somebody would come up and be like, "I'm here to network, what's your name?" And I'm like, "What? No, you can't do that. Not how that works."
turns.zh: 说真的，难以置信我参加过多少次聚会、创始人活动之类的，总有人上来就问："我是来社交的，你叫什么名字？"我直接说："什么？不行，这么做不对。"

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: I actually say I disagree with Naval on this because often, when you're part of a large organization, it's really hard to do great work and get recognized for it. You're part of a team, which is great, but it's not the same as saying having a newsletter by yourself or having a piece of content by yourself. So when I was younger, I'd be like, "Great, I'm part of a large part-
turns.zh: 其实我不同意Naval的观点，因为在大型组织中工作时，很难通过个人努力获得认可。你是团队的一员，这固然好，但与独自运营时邮件通讯或创作内容相比，效果截然不同。所以年轻时，我会想："太棒了，我加入了大团队。"

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: I don't know, I mean you guys are saying the same thing, he's just saying create value and put it out there. I don't think it's-
turns.zh: 我不知道，但你们都在说同样的道理。他强调要创造价值并主动展示。我认为这点非常重要。还有，我想说别等着创造惊人成果。往往主动迈出一步本身就能激发惊人的机遇。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, I think the putting it out there part is super interesting. And also I would just say, don't wait to create amazing things. Often just the act of putting yourself out there can just spur amazing things in itself.
turns.zh: 是啊。我尤其认为在职业生涯早期，你不会立即创造出惊人成果，所以主动接触和结交他人的价值巨大。接下来我想探讨两个方向。首先，你举办了这个关于建立人脉和社交技巧的迷你大师课。我觉得让人们回看并再次收听的关键在于，他们可能没有意识到你们两人的社交网络是多么紧密。你处于众多微型社区的核心，汇聚了最杰出的人才。我不知道你是否提过，但你运营着创作者圈、投资者、产品人员等多个微型社区，而这些社区确实发挥了作用。你可能是最善于社交的人，但人们未必知道这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And I think especially early in your career, you're not going to create amazing things immediately, so there's a lot of value to reaching out and meeting people. There's a couple of directions I want to go here. One is, so you gave this, I don't know, just mini masterclass on building a network and networking and things like that. I think what'll get people to rewind and listen to that again is I don't think people realize just how connected you two are. You're at the center of so many micro communities of the most incredible people. I don't know if you talk about this, but you run all these micro communities of incredible people in, I don't know, creator land and investors and product people and all these people and so it actually has worked. You may be the most networked person there is and I don't know if people know that.
turns.zh: 哇，真是好事吗？我不知道。这是好事吗？

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Oh, wow. Is that a good thing? I don't know. Is that-
turns.zh: 当然是好事。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: It's a good thing.
turns.zh: 是好事。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: It's a good thing. Okay, I like that, I'll go with that.
turns.zh: 这真是件好事。好吧，我喜欢这样，我选这个。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: I think the thing that, well at least with Sriram, outside of all of the masterclass stuff which I think he's particularly good at, I think the thing that Sriram, people don't realize about him is he's just inherently incredibly curious about people. He's just really just wants to know what somebody else does, who they are, what their story is. And this is not some like, "Oh, I'm going to spend 10 minutes letting them talk, I'm going to spend... he often never lets the other person talk, but when he does, he's truly-
turns.zh: 我觉得，至少就斯里拉姆而言，除了他在大师课方面特别出色之外，有一点大家可能不太了解，那就是他天生对人充满好奇。他真的很想了解别人的工作、他们的性格以及他们的故事。他不是那种会花10分钟让别人说话的人——他通常根本不让对方插话，但当他开口时，他对别人的兴趣是发自内心的。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Hold on a second right there.
turns.zh: 等一下。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: ... but he is truly curious about who they are, what their story is. By now, we've known each other for 20-ish years and this is every dinner, every event, this is just how he's wired and so you just can't fake that in building out a network. He builds a network by just wanting to know who these people are.
turns.zh: ……但他真的对别人的身份和经历充满好奇。到现在为止，我们相识了20多年了，每次聚餐、每次活动，他都是这样。这是他的天性，在拓展人脉时，你根本装不出来。他的社交之道就是想了解这些人是谁。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's beautiful.
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: The woman I married, ladies and gentlemen, right there. You marry the right person, everything else becomes [inaudible 00:28:56]. I haven't really talked about this before and I'll keep some of this slightly hidden, but I think the heart of it is I'm just curious about people, I'm just dumb about a lot of things. And I don't mean it as this false modesty way, I know a lot of folks are smarter than me. Lenny obviously is so much smarter than me at writing a Substack newsletter, it's just evident, Andrew Huberman is great at... Brian Armstrong great at building a crypto company, all these folks just evident. But what I realized is a lot of folks sometimes just want to be with other amazing peers. And one sort of hack I built over the years, I was like, "All right, let me just bring interesting people together." (00:29:34): So I bring them in, let's just say various kinds of online communities, they're probably over 100 at this point. And I say, "Okay. You trust me, you trust me and I make the rules." Everyone keeps some level of confidence, everyone is a peer, they're all accomplished in their own way, no one is rude or mean or goes off the rails. So I'm a party host, so I'm like, "Okay listen, nobody is going to get super crazy over here," but I'm also curating. I'm like, "Well, I need somebody super thoughtful, I need somebody who's a little controversial, I need somebody who's funny, I need somebody who's like the celebrity... I'm trying to put together, engineer the right vibe or the right atmosphere, but digitally, I'm very anti-social in person. And some of these just happen over time. You put together the group of people and they hang out online and over times, you have a very famous CEO becoming best friends with somebody in their early 20s who's just getting started just because they're in the same space together. (00:30:35): So I love creating those online spaces and I think it's something anybody here listening can do. Just take some of your favorite people, stick them in a WhatsApp group or a Telegram group or a Slack channel... which is by the way, Lenny's Slack, highly, highly recommend it. Lenny is great at that. But yours has hundreds of thousands of people and I think sometimes there's an intimacy from having smaller groups, like 5 people, 10 people like a shared space and then kick it off. And you'll be amazed of after a year or two, of how much intimacy and how much connection where sometimes people open up about losing their jobs or having a divorce or something really personal and intense just because of the shared trust. And I think there's something very heartwarming and fulfilling about being able to facilitate some of that.
turns.zh: 女士们先生们，就是那位我娶的女人。在座的诸位都知道。只要你嫁对了人，其他一切都会水到渠成（00:28:56处语音不清）。其实我之前从未真正谈及过这些，我会对部分细节保密，但核心要义在于，我对人充满好奇心，却在许多事情上显得愚钝无知。我这么说并非故作谦虚——我知道很多人比我聪明得多。伦尼显然比我更擅长写Substack新闻通讯，这显而易见；安德鲁·胡贝尔曼在打造加密公司方面堪称行家；布莱恩·阿姆斯特朗在创立加密公司方面更是天赋异禀——这些人都才华横溢。但我意识到，人们有时只想与杰出的同行共处。我多年来总结的一个小窍门是：“好吧，让我把有趣的人聚在一起。”（00:29:34）于是我把他们引入各类线上社区，目前这些社区已超过100个。我会说：“好吧，你们信任我，就按我的规则来。”每个人都保持着一定程度的自信，每个人都是平等的伙伴，他们都各有所长，没有人粗鲁无礼、行为失控。我就像个派对主持人，会说：“好吧，在这里大家别太疯狂。”但我同时也在精心策划。我会说：“嗯，我需要一个思想深刻的人，一个有争议性的人，一个有趣的人，一个像名人……我要组建一个合适的氛围或社区，但现实中我很不善社交。而有些事情就是顺其自然的。你把一群人聚在一起，他们在线上交流，久而久之，一位知名CEO会和一位20岁出头、刚刚起步的新人成为挚友，只因他们身处同一个领域。（00:30:35）所以我喜欢创建这些线上社区，我认为在座的每位听众都能做到。只需把你最喜欢的人聚在一起，放进WhatsApp群组、Telegram群组或Slack频道……顺便说一句，伦尼的Slack群组非常棒，强烈推荐。伦尼在这方面做得很棒。但你的社区可能有数十万成员，有时较小的群体更能营造亲密感，比如5人、10人组成的共享空间，然后逐渐发展。你会惊讶地发现，经过一两年后，人们会变得非常亲近，建立深厚的联系——有时他们会敞开心扉，谈论失业、离婚或其他私密又激烈的话题，只因彼此互相信任。我认为能促成这些交流，真的既温暖又充实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to dig into that a little bit more. You've built these incredible communities and you talked about a couple, and Aarthi, I know you also built Facebook's early community products and Clubhouse. Obviously if you had to pick one or two things you got to get right with a new community that you're just forming, what do you think those two things are or one or two things?
turns.zh: 我想再深入探讨一下。你打造了这些令人惊叹的社区，还提到了几个案例，Aarthi，我知道你也参与过Facebook早期社区产品的开发和Clubhouse项目。显然，如果要为新组建的社区确定两三个关键要素，你认为应该是什么？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Find the niche, start really small and find the niche. I think oftentimes I've seen other startup founders and I invest and advise in a lot of early stage companies. I went through Y Combinator, so I go back to YC as much as I can and go help out folks. But oftentimes I'll see people starting companies or founders coming in and being like, "I'm going to build this product that is going to cater to this community. I'm going to build this world's largest community off this kind of thing," and it almost starts at this super scaled version and then they set themselves up for failure. (00:32:14): You're almost better off doing these small, niche, non-scalable things to go find these oddball set of people who are doing this, who are really interested in this one thing and kind of scale from there and grow from there. And I think that's one big thing that when you're starting to build a community, don't start to build this super scaled community. Start with few people who are passionate about a particular problem and want to get together kind of thing. Start there. Two, I think people, and this might be a controversial thing, but I often think people don't think through monetization. If you're a community builder early on, start thinking about, if you're truly focused on this as a business, how would you actually make money off of it? (00:32:55): Oftentimes they hit some sort of scale and be like, "Crap, now what do I do? And then they're try all these options, they will have some churn and then they're like, "Oh no, but I thought this was a very sticky community." I'm like, "Yes, but it's not as sticky as this particular price tag." And so you have to start thinking through, if we hit a particular velocity, what is that going to look like? What are the things that I'm going to unlock. And think through monetization a little bit ahead of time before it comes in and becomes a crutch rather than a weapon that you can go leverage.
turns.zh:
找到细分市场，从极小规模起步，再去深挖细分领域。我发现，很多创业者在创办公司时往往会犯一个错误——他们一开始就想打造面向整个市场的产品，试图凭借某种概念迅速吸引大量用户。但这种野心勃勃的策略往往会让他们自毁长城。（00:32:14）其实，与其一开始就追求大规模扩张，不如先专注于小而精、非标准化的项目，找到那些对特定领域充满热情、渴望深度交流的用户群体。以此为基础，逐步扩大规模。这是社区建设中一个关键的启示：不要一开始就试图打造面向大众的社区，而是要从少数对某个问题充满热情、渴望交流的用户群体入手。  

第二点（00:32:55），我认为（这或许会引发争议）很多创业者在商业化策略上考虑不周。早期社区建设者应该提前思考：如果把这当作一项业务，如何从中获利？他们往往等到规模上来了，才惊呼“糟糕，现在该怎么办？”然后尝试各种变现方案，遭遇用户流失后，又感叹“天啊，我以为这个社区黏性很强”。我会回应：“没错，但你设定的这个价格标签并不足以支撑黏性。”因此，必须提前规划：当用户规模达到某个阶段时，商业模式会呈现怎样的形态？哪些功能可以解锁？提前构思变现路径，才能让它成为利器而非阻碍。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: But I want to say, Aarthi is kind of the creator of Facebook Stars and of so much of the thinking there and I can see her go super deep on this. Of course on everything she said, I have a slightly different framework. First of all, I really don't like the word community because the word community, the word networking, the word platform is a little abstract and it can mean a lot of things. And I like to think of things like a dinner party or church or things that seem more tangible and people know, "Okay, I know exactly what that is." So when I think of a community or starting one, I think first of all, it's a party. And you're first starting off, you're like, "All right, what is a vibe?" (00:33:57): For example and this is also true for every social media platform where if you can be a crazy, people are dancing on bars, having a great time, getting really drunk party or you can have a really formal dinner where everyone is seated, there is plates with name tags and there's a clinking of glasses and you have to dress up. And they're both fine, they're both fun in their own way, but you need to tell people, as the host, which one it is. And by the way, I think one of the things that Twitter didn't get right in the original days which some of the other apps did, it never told people what kind of party it was. It like, "Are we going to Michelin star restaurant where sit down or it's a sports bar after the Super Bowl and you can go crazy?" And if you don't do that, people make up their own rules. That's number one. (00:34:37): The second part is as the host, you have to curate the original set of people and you need a mix, this is super important. I think sometimes people do this thing where they either optimize for "interesting famous people" or they get the most talkative lot of people. And I actually read a bunch of books on hosting great dinner parties, I actually have some interesting suggestions there and it'll say like, "Well, you need a mix." For example, in any organization, let's say you're the VP that everyone knows about, but that VP doesn't have the time to maybe participate on a WhatsApp channel or a Slack channel and chit-chat all the time or show up for everything. And then maybe you need the really boisterous young BD exec who's out and about and meeting everybody. You need that person, you need somebody who's quiet and thoughtful. You need to merge different kinds of energy and that's almost an alchemy and that's more art than science. You have to start there. (00:35:27): Third I think is as the host, you have to have a sixth sense of how is a community feeling at any given point in time? Are two people dominating the conversation? That person hasn't said anything in a while. One of the things I like to when somebody joins a group or one of these places, I try and get them into a question which they will feel happy about because you know what happens the very first time you walk into a party? You look around, you're like, "I don't know anybody here. Oh gosh, okay. I know this one person and I'm going to go talk to them," and you just feel nervous. I'm trying to break that. For example, if you walk in a place and you didn't know anybody, Lenny is actually very good at being social, but I'd be like, "Hey. Lenny has one of the most popular things on Substack and he just wrote [inaudible 00:36:04]. I'm just giving you an opening, you to feel comfortable and that's another part. (00:36:08): The third part I love is rituals and religions do a great job of this, which is do something every month. There's a little group I hosted some of my friends and during all of COVID, we did a Zoom meeting every Tuesday evening. And that was a ritual, it had nothing, it's just Zoom meeting with a bunch of friends, people can share-
turns.zh:
但我想说，Aarthi可以说是Facebook Stars的缔造者，也是其背后的诸多理念的源泉。我能感受到她对此有着深刻的见解。当然，对于她提到的所有观点，我都有一些略微不同的看法。首先，我不太喜欢“社区”这个词，因为“社区”、“社交平台”之类的概念太抽象，可能涵义多样。我更倾向于把它们看作是更具体的事物，比如晚宴、教堂活动之类的，人们一听就能明白其含义。所以当我思考社区或如何创建社区时，我首先会想到这是一场聚会。刚开始时，你会想，“氛围如何？”（00:33:57）：举个例子，Twitter在初期就没能正确处理这一点，而其他一些应用却做得很好——它从未明确告知用户聚会的性质。比如，“我们是去米其林星级餐厅享用正餐，还是去超级碗后狂欢的体育酒吧尽情狂欢？”如果不明确规则，人们就会自行设定规则。这是首要问题。

（00:34:37）第二点是，作为主办方，你需要精心挑选最初的参与者，并确保他们形成多样化的组合。这点至关重要。我发现有些人要么只招募“有趣的名人”，要么找最健谈的人参加。我曾研读过许多关于举办精彩晚宴的书籍，其中提到：“你需要多样化的人员组合。” 比如，在任何组织中，如果你是一位众所周知的副总裁，但他可能没有时间参与WhatsApp或Slack频道的闲聊，也无法出席所有活动。这时，你就需要一位活泼外向、四处社交的年轻业务开发主管。还需要安静内省的思考者。要融合不同类型的能量，这几乎是门艺术而非科学。这一点至关重要。

（00:35:27）第三点是，作为主办方，你必须具备敏锐的直觉，感知社区在任何特定时刻的氛围如何？是否有两个人主导了整个对话？是否有人许久未发言？当有人加入一个群组或平台时，我会尝试引导他们参与一个让他们感到自在的话题。比如，走进一个陌生的场合时，Lenny确实很善于社交，但我会先说：“嘿，Lenny在Substack上有一篇很受欢迎的文章，他刚写了[此处缺失部分]。”我这样做就是为了打破他们的拘谨感。这也是关键之处。

（00:36:08）第三点我很推崇的是仪式感。宗教在这方面做得很好，比如每月固定举办某种活动。有一个我组织的小组活动
新冠疫情期间，我的一些朋友和我每周二晚上都会开一次Zoom会议。这成了我们固定的活动，没有什么特别的仪式感，就是一群朋友聚在一起开个Zoom会议，大家可以互相分享各自的生活近况。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: And people would just bring their glass of wine or bring their kids in and there's no structured agenda. But people started looking forward to it through the pandemic and stuff and we would be like, "Oh my God, it's Tuesday. You know this evening, we are going to go do this thing." And it was a really great way to go build that community and I totally agree with that.
turns.zh: 人们只是会带上一杯葡萄酒，或者带着孩子来参加，没有固定的议程。但在疫情期间及之后，人们开始期待每周二的聚会。我们会兴奋地说：“天哪，又到周二了！今晚我们要去参加这个活动了。” 这确实是建立社区感的绝佳方式，我完全赞同这种做法。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan

turns.zh: 是啊，我看到莱尼在Slack上把这事儿做得特别棒。

Interesting point, a four person dinner, very different from an eight person dinner, very different from a 20 person thing where people hang out, very different from, once you start getting hundreds of thousands, the things you're willing to share, worrying about being judged. turns.zh: 另一个有趣的矛盾和挑战在于如何发展社区。我认为存在……一个有趣的点——四人晚餐与八人晚餐大不相同，八人晚餐又和20人的社交聚会不同。一旦人数达到数十万，人们愿意分享的内容就会有所不同，还要担心被评判。所以我一直在努力打造更私密的不同空间，但这又是一个完全不同的议题。所以我觉得如果你想创建一个社区，我会说挑选合适的人，设定基调，自己深度参与其中，这才是关键。

turns.en: Dude, no, this is really important because I think what stops a lot of people is, I've had probably 100 plus conversations where somebody who's incredibly accomplished will come to me and they'll be like, "Hey, I want to get on Twitter, I want write content or I want to Substack or I want to do a podcast." I'm like, "Great." They're like, "But I don't know what to say, I look dumb, I don't want to get judged." But I'm like, "No, you're so accomplished," and it is the fear of being judged that so often stops people. So whenever I hear that word cringe, I'm like, "No, no, no, that's actually fine, you're fine. You'll figure it out," and here's why I say that. (00:40:30): Number one is what the most important thing and even, listen, if you just remember one thing from this whole thing is just get started and do something every single day. And this sounds so basic, like Aarthi and I have is a running joke where it's like it's diet and exercise is what we say. It's like we are talking to people about how do you get healthy and you have the 100 different things you can do or podcasts you can listen to, but most of it's like, "Well, diet and exercise." And with creating content, diet and exercise, you just write a piece of content every single day because what's going to happen is it builds muscle, it gets you familiar with the medium and you start understanding what works in that medium and what doesn't and you start building reps. (00:41:08): You know who never works out in my opinion? Is somebody who'll think for weeks, build up an amazing tweetstorm, blog post, newsletter, whatever it may be and then stops because the effort is so high. So I'm like, "One, do something every single day." The second part of it is, I actually think you don't have to talk about what you accomplish, you only have to talk about you. And by the way, this is going to sound very froufrou, but you are the best you out there. So for example-
turns.zh: 老兄，不，这真的很重要。我觉得阻碍很多人的是，我可能已经和100多个非常有成就的人聊过，他们会来找我说，“嘿，我想上推特，我想写内容，或者想做Substack，或者想做播客。”我说，“太好了。”他们会说，“但我不知道说什么，我看起来很傻，我不想被评判。”但我会说，“不，你太有成就了，”而正是害怕被评判的心理常常阻止人们行动。所以每当我听到‘尴尬’这个词时，我都会说，‘不，不，不，这其实没关系，你很好。你会找到方法的，’以下是我这么说的原因。（00:40:30）：第一点是最重要的，听着，如果你从这整个讨论中只记住一件事，那就是开始行动，每天做点什么。这听起来很基础，就像阿尔提和我经常开玩笑说的，就是饮食和锻炼。我们和人们谈论如何变得健康时，他们会列出100种不同的方法或可以收听的播客，但大多数都是‘好吧，那就饮食和锻炼吧。’对于创作内容也是如此，饮食和锻炼，你每天就写一篇内容，因为这样做会锻炼你的技能，让你熟悉这个媒介，开始理解什么在这种媒介上有效，什么无效，然后开始积累经验。（00:41:08）：你知道在我看来谁从不锻炼吗？就是那些会花几周时间精心策划一个精彩的推特风暴、博客文章、新闻通讯之类的，但因为投入太大而半途而废的人。所以我说，‘第一，每天做点什么。’第二点是，我认为你不必谈论自己的成就，你只需要谈论你自己就好。顺便说一句，这听起来可能很虚伪，但你就是最棒的自己。所以举个例子——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Wow, okay.

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: ... let's say you are a 21-year-old PM, fresh out of school, first year... by the way, we were all that. I was a 21-year-old PM at one time, Lenny would've been too, lots of others. First you'll see a lot of people who have been through journey and there are others like you. Second is you just talk about your journey, talk about what you're doing, talk about what you're learning. Because what often you're trying to do when you're creating content is to build a relationship with people. So when Charli D'Amelio dances on TikTok, she's not saying she's a professional dancer, she's saying, "I'm relatable, I'm just like somebody you would be friends with next door, I'm just like you." And so then people start connecting with you on that front, if you're authentic and you're doing a good job, and so everybody listening to this should be able to create content.
turns.zh: 比如说，你是一位21岁的产品经理，刚毕业第一年……顺便说一句，我们当年也都是这样的。我自己曾经也是21岁的产品经理，Lenny当时也会是，还有很多其他人。首先，你会看到很多已经走过这段路的人，还有和你们情况相似的新人。其次，你只需要分享自己的经历，谈谈你正在做的事情，聊聊你正在学习的东西。因为当你创作内容时，最重要的就是和用户建立联系。比如说Charli D'Amelio在TikTok上跳舞时，她不是在说自己是专业舞者，而是传达出“我很亲切，我就像你隔壁的邻居一样，和你很合拍”的感觉。这样一来，只要你真诚且表现出色，就能和听众建立联系。听众中应该每个人都能创作内容。

I think at the end of the day, you have to persevere, I think I give a lot more words to people who are just persevering and showing up every day, but I do think there should be a level of self-awareness for people where it's like, "Man, this is not great.
