turns.en: I agree with you, but I think when people mean cringey... okay, I'll see this. What people think they say cringey, it's like our peer group thinks that this content is too basic-
turns.zh: 我同意你的观点，但我觉得当人们说内容尴尬时……好的，我明白了。人们认为内容尴尬，可能是因为我们的同行群体觉得这内容太基础了——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: But everybody has that, whether you say it out loud or not.
turns.zh: 但每个人都会经历这种情况，无论你是否说出来。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Well, I'll give you a story. So I spent years, I'd be like, "I'm a PM leader, I run organization, I should write smart PM things. I should write the kinds of things that Lenny writes." For example, I'll say that, "Lenny's Post the other week from Duolingo is... I was so jealous. I was like, "Man, this is the kind of content... I would be like, "It's amazing, banger post." But the problem was when you start doing that, you start censoring yourself. And I'll say, I've written a lot of posts over the years and I'll try and sound smart, I have a great intellectual framework in some of this work, but you know what my most popular post and tweetstorm of all time is? It is how to write a cold email. (00:43:48): And when I wrote that tweetstorm, I was like, "Man, I'm going to sound so dumb," because Lenny doesn't need to know how to write a cold email and neither does the VCs I work with, everyone knows that. But the thing is, what is obvious to you and may seem cringey to your peers is definitely not obvious to a lot of people and they will connect to you, they will relate to you. When somebody says like, "Well, is it too basic? How do I get started with my job?" I'm like, "No, there's a lot of people who this is not obvious to," and I'll just put myself out there and what's the worst thing? Somebody thinks you're moron? That's fine. You put some new piece of content out there the next day and they'll fix it or you can just ignore that.
turns.zh: 好吧，我给你讲个故事。多年来，我一直想：“我是个产品经理，管理团队，我应该写些聪明的产品经理内容，应该写Lenny那样的文章。” 比如，我会说，“Lenny前几天在Duolingo上的那篇帖子……我太羡慕了。我当时就想，‘天啊，这就是我想要的那种内容……’” 但问题是，当你开始这样做时，就会自我审查。我写了很多帖子，试图显得高深莫测，有些作品确实有很好的知识框架，但你知道我最受欢迎的帖子和推文风暴是什么？是如何写冷邮件。（00:43:48）当我写那篇推文时，我想，“天啊，我会显得很傻”，因为Lenny不需要知道如何写冷邮件，我合作的风投公司的人也不需要，每个人都知道。但问题是，对你来说显而易见、在同行眼中可能觉得尴尬的内容，对很多人来说却不明显，他们会与你产生共鸣。当有人问，“嗯，这太基础了吧？我该如何开始我的工作？” 我会说，“不，有很多人还不懂这些。”然后我就大胆尝试，最坏的情况是什么？有人觉得你是个白痴？那也没关系。第二天你再发布新内容，他们会纠正错误，或者你可以直接忽略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's a lot of really good nuggets here. I think the only area maybe we disagree and we should move on, but this is [inaudible 00:44:29].
turns.zh: 我觉得这里有很多很棒的观点。但可能有一点我们意见不一致，我们还是先放一放吧，不过这部分（00:44:29处）可能需要调整语气。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Listen to me, Lenny, come on. Your podcast is too friendly otherwise, let's listen.
turns.zh: 听我说，莱尼，别这样。你的播客太友好了，不然我们就听听看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My feeling is I think for helping you do better work kind of content, like entertainment anyone could do no problem, you could be awesome at it, is I feel like you need to do something in your career first before you can start speaking to, "Here's things I've learned and here's what works and here's what doesn't work." I think I wouldn't spend a lot of time sharing all your wisdom before you've done a thing and been successful in some way.
turns.zh: 我的感觉是，如果你想帮助别人做得更好——比如娱乐类内容，任何人都能做得不错，你可能在这方面很出色——但我觉得你需要先在自己的职业生涯中有所建树，然后再开始说：“我学到了这些，哪些方法有效，哪些没用。”我觉得在你有所成就、取得成功之前，不应该急于分享你所有的智慧。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah. I actually think you make a very interesting point, which is I think a lot of people online LARP, live action role-play, as somebody else which is like you trying to project a persona or a career point that you are not at and you know it, we know it, you probably admit you know it-
turns.zh: 是啊。我其实觉得你提出了一个很有意思的观点，那就是很多人在网上把自己装扮成别人，比如试图塑造一个不真实的形象或职业定位，但你自己清楚，我们也知道，你可能也承认这一点——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: And also for that kind of content, everyone can tell. I think it just comes off as not authentic. I mean I feel like the universe figures itself out over time, but I do think there is a level of, just because Sriram thinks no content is cringey does not mean people all feel that way. You can't just magically just wipe that out. I feel like everyone just feels that way, whether or not you say it out loud. I do think there is a process of iteration and acknowledging that, "Yeah, okay, this is bad, but I'm going to put this out there anyway and we'll just keep working on this," and coming back to it. (00:45:46): I really appreciate people who would just do that and just keep coming back to it every day and like Rocky style, chip away at things. I really have appreciation for those folks because it's hard. I've realized over time that everyone is deeply feeling as if they're imposters and we talked about this. Imposter syndrome is so real, it is so gut-wrenchingly real that it's not just every one person, it's most people I think. So to be able to overcome that threshold and look at your amazing peers and your seniors and everybody else and then still be able to put yourself out there, I think we have to really appreciate that and help them go iterate and just get better over time.
turns.zh: 而且对于这类内容，大家都能看出来不真实。我觉得这让人感觉不真诚。我的意思是，宇宙会随着时间自然发展，但我确实认为有一种程度的真诚。即使斯里拉姆认为没有内容是尴尬的，但并不意味着所有人都这么认为。你不能就这样神奇地抹去这种感觉。我觉得每个人都会有这种感觉，无论你是否说出来。我确实认为这是一个迭代和自我承认的过程，比如，“好吧，这确实不行，但我还是要把它发布出去，然后继续改进。”（00:45:46）：我真的很欣赏那些每天坚持迭代、不断进步的人，就像《洛奇》那种坚持不懈的精神。我真的很欣赏这些人，因为这很难。我逐渐意识到，每个人都深深感到自己是个冒牌货，我们也讨论过这个问题。冒牌综合症太真实了，太令人心痛地真实了，它不只是个别人的问题，我觉得大多数人都有这种感觉。所以能够克服这个障碍，看着你出色的同行、前辈和其他人，而仍然能勇敢地展现自己，我觉得我们真的应该为此心怀感激，并帮助他们不断迭代、不断进步。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, I agree. One tiny story before we wrap on this topic, which is I was talking to somebody who's four or five years into their career as a PM and they'd written this post on LinkedIn which is full of cringey content, by the way. Okay, let me say it, LinkedIn has a lot of cringey PM content-
turns.zh: 是的，我同意。在结束这个话题之前，我想分享一个小故事。有一个做项目经理四五年的人，在领英上发了一篇帖子，里面全是尴尬的内容。好吧，我得说一句，领英上有很多尴尬的项目经理内容——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Wow, look at Sriram.
turns.zh: 哇，看看斯里拉姆。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: ... I'm sorry LinkedIn folks. And it was one of the things about how do you set product strategy as an organization and I was like, I called them, I was like, "Dude, come on. You're four years into your role, nobody believes that you actually are driving this from a place of actually really knowing it. And that is fine if you're learning, but you are trying to project this person you're not." But the thing which I was talking to him, I was like, "I know you've done this amazing deep dive on this other niche topic. You've gone out, you read all the posts, go write about that because you are an expert legitimately in something you think is niche, as opposed to a fake expert on this other thing you want to be." (00:47:17): He went and wrote this follow-up post on something very niche and that went really popular because the truth is, there's not a lot of great content out there, especially great content from people who actually done the thing. You'd be surprised how niche you can be, but if you actually done the work, talk to a people, aggregated some posts, people come seek you out and you don't have to do it. So anyway, so lots of LARPing, lots of cringey LinkedIn content for sure.
turns.zh: 抱歉了，领英的朋友们。这事关如何从组织层面制定产品策略。我当时就想，"老兄，别这样了。你担任这个角色已经四年了，没人相信你真的在以深刻理解为基础来推动这项工作。如果你只是在学习，那倒也无妨，但你却试图假装成一个真正的专家。"不过我跟他聊的时候，我说，"我知道你对另一个小众领域做了深入研究。你出去调研，阅读所有相关帖子，然后写了篇文章，因为你确实是某个被视为小众领域的专家，而不是在其他领域冒充专家。" （00:47:17）他照做了，写了一篇关于小众领域的后续文章，收获了大量关注，因为现实是，优质内容实在太少了，尤其是那些真正做过相关工作的内容。人们会惊讶于你能做到多么小众，但只要你真正下了功夫，采访过相关人士，整合过大量帖子，人们自然会主动找你，而你根本无需主动推广。所以总之，很多人在虚伪行事，在领英上发布尴尬内容，这确实很常见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to close this out, I 100% agree with the idea that people should be just trying stuff, writing, sharing stuff on Twitter, LinkedIn, just get it out of there, don't be afraid because that's how you start down this road. I was going to go in a different direction, but you mentioned imposter syndrome and I'm curious, have you two dealt with imposter syndrome and-
turns.zh: 最后说一句，我完全赞同人们应该多去尝试、写作、在推特和领英上分享内容的观点，不要害怕，因为这就是你踏上这条道路的起点。我原本想转换话题，但你提到了冒名顶替综合症，我很好奇，你们俩是否也深受其扰？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Oh, yeah. We have and I still, I don't know about Sriram. Sriram comes off as so much more confident and has so much gravitas that nobody ever thinks of it, but we both do, we both deeply have imposter syndrome. Every single day, anything we do, we look at ourselves, we are creators, we have this show on YouTube and then we look around at everybody else who have millions of subscribers and followers and everything and we are like, "Why are we creators? This is not a thing. We should not be doing this stuff. I just think people haven't been honest with us on how much we suck." It's like you have these loops in your head and then every once in a while, you'll see a comment being like, "This was amazing. I just had to stop doing what I was doing to listen to this whole thing. It was so valuable for me." And you're like, "Oh, okay. We are not all the bad. That's, I think, okay." (00:48:48): So we go through this a lot. For the longest time, I had really severe imposter syndrome through school, college, getting into Microsoft. Even after I got through the Microsoft, which we were one of the youngest product managers there, I still was like, "Oh, someday they're going to figure out that this was all... they'll know the real me and they'll be like, 'Oh man, we made this mistake with her.'" And it was just such a real crippling thing for me. Even now I feel like maybe it's not 100% true, but I can kind of see the gradients there, so very real thing.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。我们确实深受其扰，不过我不确定斯里拉姆的感受。他给人的感觉自信得多、气场也强得多，别人从不质疑他，但我们都深受其扰。每天做任何事时，我们都会审视自己。我们是创作者，运营着YouTube节目，然后环顾四周，看到那些拥有数百万订阅者和粉丝的人，就会想，"我们为什么要做创作者？这根本不算什么。我们不该做这些事的。我觉得人们从未诚实地告诉我们我们有多糟糕。"这就像大脑里不断循环的自我怀疑。偶尔会看到评论说，"太棒了。我不得不停下手头的事来听完整个内容。这对我太有价值了。"这时你会想，"哦，原来我们没那么糟糕。这还不错。" （00:48:48）所以我们经常经历这样的循环。在校期间、大学时期、进入微软后，我都深受冒名顶替综合症困扰。即使在微软成为最年轻的产品经理之一后，我仍会想，"总有一天他们会发现这一切都是……他们会发现真实的我，然后说，'天哪，我们当时真是选错人了。' 这对我来说真是毁灭性的打击。即使现在，我觉得这可能不完全属实，但我能隐约看到其中的递进过程，所以这确实是个很真实的问题。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, it's so true. I have a hack or a technique of how to get over imposter syndrome. But I'll just say, and this is just if folks here feel it, every new job I've been in, I have always felt that I didn't deserve to be there and I mean I genuinely. When I joined Microsoft, I was a young student, I was like, "I don't know anything. These folks are professional, they've been doing this job for years." When I moved to the US I said, "Look, my accent is super intense, I'm Indian, these folks have been doing this for many years, they have very different lifestyles, I don't know what I'm doing here." When I move to Silicon Valley, I got no hired by probably four or five different companies and one of them told me, "You work for Microsoft so you can't really cut it in Silicon Valley because you're from Seattle," which I'll never forget. (00:50:07): And I look at the person from LinkedIn from time to time, I'm very typically like, "Well, I've cut it now," and I'm very petty that way. And then of course and then when I start running large organizations, several hundred people or more, I was like, "I've never done this before." I'm in a meeting, everyone is looking to me, "Do they know that I've not done this before? Because I haven't done this before and can they tell?" And it's every step of the way. So it just pushes every step of the way and in the beginning, it was quite crippling, but over time, you build things to help you. And I think for those listening, if you feel this way, the thing I've learned to do is you have to retreat to a place where you feel real mastery of. So for example, when I was at Microsoft, I was like, "Well, I don't speak the language very well, English," and I had an accent, et cetera, but I knew that I was the most online developer person out there. (00:50:57): I knew every single online community, I was very plugged into open source, so in every meeting when the topic would come to, "Hey, what is happening with Ruby on Rails?" I was like, "I know this better than everybody else," and I learned to put together a presentation. Because then you start with the base of something that you feel super comfortable in and you build from that. And what you realize when you build from that is you are like, "Oh, actually you know what? People really respect that and they react to that." And I also learned not to do other things. For example, for them for years where I would listen to people from a certain academic background or I'll be like, "I wish I could do slide decks like they could," or, "I wish I could have these intentional... but I was like, "That doesn't really matter. You just need to come from a place where you are confident you've done the work." (00:51:39): So if you folks are listening and you feel imposter syndrome, next time you walk into a meeting, just think about, "Okay, this is a place where I know I spend so many nights and weekends," and it can be super tiny, it can be one little button, one customer, but you've done the work, you've had multiple conversations, it is [inaudible 00:51:54]. And you start from there, you talk about that and you build out from that and you will feel comfortable. So I've done that in pretty much every role now and I still catch myself doing-
turns.zh: 是啊，这话太对了。我倒是有一套克服冒名顶替综合症的窍门。不过说实话，如果在座各位有共鸣的话，我在每份新工作中都曾深切感受到自己不配待在那里——我是说，我真心这么觉得。刚加入微软时，我还是个年轻学生，心想：“我啥都不懂。这些人都是专业人士，干这行多年了。” 搬到美国后，我又说：“看，我口音超重，还是印度人，人家在这儿干了好多年了，生活方式完全不同，我在这儿能行吗？” 去硅谷后，大概有四五家公司面试我，其中一家甚至说：“你来自西雅图，又在微软工作过，在硅谷根本混不下去。” 这话我永生难忘。（00:50:07） 我时不时会看看领英上的前同事，总会想：“哼，我现在已经成功了。” 说实话，我还挺小心眼的。后来管理几百人的大团队时，又会想：“我从没干过这事啊。” 开会时大家都盯着我看：“他们知道我没经验吗？因为我确实没经验啊，他们能看出来吗？” 每一步都充满挑战。刚开始真的很煎熬，但随着时间推移，你总能找到应对之法。对于听众们，如果你们也有这种感受，我学到的是退回到自己擅长的领域。比如在微软时，虽然英语口语不行，还有口音等问题，但我深知自己是最懂在线开发的人。我熟悉每个社区，深耕开源领域。每次会议提到“Ruby on Rails最近动态如何？”时，我都能说：“我比任何人都清楚。” 我还学会了不去攀比。比如多年来，我会羡慕某些学术背景的人的幻灯片制作能力，但后来意识到这无关紧要——你只需从自己擅长的领域出发，逐步积累。这样你会发现人们真的尊重你的专业能力，并给予积极反馈。（00:51:39） 所以听众们，如果你们也有冒名顶替综合症，下次开会时，不妨想想：“好吧，这里是我无数个夜晚和周末投入的领域。” 哪怕只是一颗小小的螺丝，一位客户，但你付出了努力，进行了多次交流，这就是成功的基石。从此你就能以此为基础，逐步建立自信，自然而然地游刃有余了。如今我几乎在每个职位上都践行了这些方法，但偶尔还是会发现自己还在纠结——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah, I think for me, when I was a first time founder, I definitely felt that way and there was all this, at that time, which was conventional wisdom. Nobody we knew at that time were founders, it's not our friend circle, they all worked in medium to big companies. My family, nobody has ever been a founder, entrepreneur, it's not a thing. And so when I started this I was like, "Oh my God, I'm making a mistake." But then you read all these people tweeting or writing posts, being like, "If you're a founder you'll be really good at fundraising. Best founders learn how to... I sucked at fundraising. I was so bad at it. It was just like, "Oh, you have to be able to tell your story." (00:52:41): I tried. I email like 250 founders, took 85 meetings and 50 plus second meetings and then got 30 checks. This was my seed round which took eight months to close or something and I was like, "Oh my God, I'm so bad at this. I should just give up right now." And then I started building this startup and I was like, "Actually I'm really, really good at understanding customer acquisition and really trying to find creative ways to cheaply acquire customers." And I kind of started putting together playbooks on it, what I can go do there and I tried this, I tried this, then I started talking to few for our own investors and I'm like, "I don't know if your portfolio companies are finding this useful, but I tried these tactics." And they were like, "Oh my God, I'd never heard of that." (00:53:28): And so I realized that that's the one place I could be really good at and I can grow my business in a really profitable way very quickly. And then investors started talking to me about other companies and all of that stuff and it became a thing and that helped me get more confidence over time. It was like, who cares if I can't do these other things? I can do these few things and this is really, really important to build a sustainable business and I think I can do that. And that for me kind of helped me get over it. It's not anyone telling me, "Don't worry, you'll be good at it," that never helped, it was just I had to do it myself to figure it out.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得对我来说，当我第一次创业时，确实有这种感觉。当时社会上流传着很多所谓的"常识"。那个时候，我们认识的人里没人是创业者，这根本不属于我们的社交圈，他们大多在大中型公司工作。我的家人从未有过创业者或企业家，这个概念对他们来说很陌生。所以当我刚开始创业时，我就在想：“天啊，我这是犯了一个大错。” 但后来我看到很多人在推特上发帖或写文章，说：“如果你是一名创业者，你就会很擅长融资。最优秀的创业者会学会如何……我很不擅长融资。简直就像‘你必须会讲好你的故事’。” （00:52:41）我尝试了各种方法：给250位创业者发邮件，参加了85次会议，其中50多次是二次会面，最终拿到了30笔投资。这是我的种子轮融资，用了八个月才完成，我当时就想：“天啊，我太不擅长这事了。我应该现在就放弃吧。” 然后我开始打造这家初创公司，发现自己其实非常擅长理解客户获取策略，善于寻找低成本获取客户的创新方法。我开始整理相关指南，尝试各种方法，最后和几位潜在投资者交流时说：“我不知道你们投资组合中的公司是否觉得这些策略有用，但我确实尝试过这些方法。” 他们惊讶地说：“天啊，我从没听说过这些策略。” （00:53:28）于是我意识到，这正是我真正擅长的领域，我能以快速且盈利的方式发展业务。后来投资者开始向我推荐其他公司，整个局面逐渐明朗，这让我逐渐建立了信心。就好像，“其他技能不行又怎样？我擅长这几项，而这对建立可持续的业务至关重要，我相信自己能做到。” 这对我来说就是克服恐惧的关键。那些说“别担心，总会成功的”之类的话根本没用，真正有效的是亲自实践、摸索总结。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting both of your pieces of advice is find the thing you're actually good at and then just lean into that as much as possible. That's something I learned from an executive coach I worked with once that you have strengths, you have weaknesses, you can accomplish almost all the things you want accomplish through the lens of the strengths without using those weaknesses as much and that really was pretty transformative.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，你们两人的建议都是找到自己真正擅长的领域，然后尽可能深耕其中。这是我从一位高管教练那里学到的。他说，每个人都有优势和劣势，但通过聚焦优势、减少依赖劣势，你几乎能实现所有目标。这真是让我受益匪浅。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: That's actually such a profound point and I wish somebody had told me that earlier in my career because early in my career, I would get all this advice like, "Oh, Sriram is too loud and too boisterous." And the thing is, nobody I know has ever become successful by trying to fix their weaknesses, it's just impossible. The only way you succeed is one, you might need to mitigate some of them, especially if they're really, really holding you back. But you have to lean into your strengths, which is a weird thing because I think when we do performance feedback, it's feedback and so much time we are like, "Well, these are all the good things and then let's talk about the ways you know can improve." (00:54:53): It's almost the flip time and I think if you're doing performance feedback, you'll be like, "Well, these are things you're really good at, let's make you even much better at that. Let's make you fly faster, run harder, close the deal, write better code." Oh yeah, and some people are mad at you for these things. You should watch it and maybe fix some if it's really bad, but that's not what's going to pull you ahead. It's the superpowers that's going to really pull you ahead, so let's focus on that.
turns.zh:
实际上，这是一个非常深刻的观点。我真希望在职业生涯早期就有人能告诉我这一点，因为那时我总会听到诸如“Sriram太吵闹、太张扬了”之类的批评。问题是，我认识的所有成功人士，从来都不是靠改正自己的弱点才成功的，这根本不可能。成功的关键在于：一方面，你可能需要弱化某些弱点，尤其是那些真正拖后腿的；但另一方面，你必须充分发挥自己的优势。这听起来有点反常，因为在绩效评估时，我们通常会把重点放在改进弱点上。但我认为，在绩效评估中，应该先肯定对方的优势，再谈改进之处。这才是正确的顺序。

（00:54:53）：但现实中很多评估反过来了。你应该先夸奖对方的优点，再指出改进空间。比如，“你在这方面做得很棒，让我们一起把它做得更好。你要飞得更高、跑得更快、达成交易、写出更好的代码。” 是的，有些人可能会因此批评你，但这些批评并不能推动你前进。真正能推动你前进的，是你的核心优势，所以我们应该专注于此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The way I think about that is the weaknesses can't be liabilities, you can't just get on stage and melt and explode, but you don't have to be amazing. As long as you can email really well, write documents really well, communicate in other ways if that's a strength. One last trick while we're on this topic, I was just reading Hunter Walk's blog and he shared a cool trick for imposter syndrome where you just have to ask yourself, "Am I so good at pretending that people don't see what's actually happening? Am I actually that good to being this imposter? Probably not, the people can tell," and it's really unlikely you're actually an imposter.
turns.zh: 是啊。我对此的看法是，弱点不应成为阻碍你成功的负担。你不可能上台就崩溃，但你也不必追求完美。只要你能出色地发邮件、写文件，或者通过其他方式有效沟通，这就足够了。顺便说一句，我刚读了Hunter Walk的博客，他分享了一个应对冒名顶替综合症的妙招：你只需问自己：“我是否善于伪装，让别人看不出我的真实状态？我是否真的在扮演这个冒名顶替者？很可能不是，别人能看穿的。”所以你根本就不是冒名顶替者。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Also, by the way, the reality is and this a cliche is people are just not thinking about you.
turns.zh: 而且，现实情况是——虽然听起来老生常谈——但人们根本不会关注你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: That's true. Yeah, you're giving other people too much credit that they're focused on somebody else. Everyone is so busy focusing on themselves and their own insecurities and fear and just living life. And think about ourselves, when was the last time we thought about somebody else and were like, "That person, probably an imposter"? We just don't have the time for it.
turns.zh: 确实如此。是啊，你太高估别人对你的关注度了。大家都忙着关注自己，处理自己的不安和恐惧，过自己的生活。想想我们自己，什么时候最后一次思考别人并想：“那个人可能是个冒名顶替者？”我们根本没时间这么做。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, I've been thinking about me this whole time.
turns.zh: 是啊，我一直都在反思自己。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: I am not surprised.
turns.zh: 我一点也不惊讶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You guys are hilarious. There's something I actually along these lines I was going to ask about. I remember, Sriram, when you were just getting out of the companies you worked at, you made this point that you were an IC and you were in these meetings where people are reviewing your work and they're making decisions and you're the person presenting. And then all of a sudden, you're the person reviewing all their work and making the decisions and no one trained you to be that person where you're like, "Oh my God, I'm that person they're all looking for for all these answers?" And I'm curious just how you worked through that and what advice you'd have for people that are maybe going through that transition?
turns.zh: 你们太逗了。其实我正好有类似的想法想问。我记得，Sriram，你刚离开前公司时，提到自己作为IC参加会议，别人在评审你的工作，做决策，而你负责展示。然后突然间，你成了评审所有人工作、做决策的人，却没人教过你如何胜任这个角色，你会想：“天啊，我就是别人找答案的对象？”我很好奇你当时是如何应对的，对那些正经历这种转变的人有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good question. First of all, it's kind of a jarring change because you realize, "Well, I have power, but I'm also called upon to do a bunch of things," because no meeting, let's call it an exec review, let's say and you're the exec they're presenting too. It doesn't really matter what your title is. All of a sudden, you're having to do a bunch of things. You're making decisions, but you're also providing feedback, sometimes explicitly, sometimes implicitly. (00:57:10): You might piss off somebody by naming somebody and not naming the other person, you might piss off somebody by not inviting them to the meeting. You might have to feel like, "Well, I really want to overrule this person, but if I do, they might get mad at me." And there are so many different things which you have to keep in your head as well as like, "Is this the right path for the team, for the company," or whatever the situation is and it can be really overwhelming. And I learned a lot of how to do great exec reviews from my time at Facebook, from Zuck and from Andrew Bosworth. Andrew Bosworth, Boz, has some great posts on his site, boz.com, about how to do reviews and-
turns.zh:
是啊，这是个好问题。首先，这确实是个令人不适的转变，因为你会意识到：“好吧，我手握权力，但又被要求做一堆事情。” 比如在一场高管评审会上，你既是被评估的对象，也是评审者。这时头衔并不重要——突然间，你就得处理各种事务。既要做决策，又要提供反馈，有时是明示的，有时是暗示的。（00:57:10）你可能会因为点名某人而忽略另一个人而得罪人，也可能因为不邀请某人参加会议而招致不满。你甚至得考虑：“我真想否决这个人的提议，但那样他们可能会生我的气。” 此外，你还得时刻保持清醒，判断这对团队、对公司是否正确，或者根据具体情况做出判断——这真的会让人应接不暇。  

我在Facebook工作时，从扎克伯格和安德鲁·博斯沃斯那里学到了很多如何开展高管评审的技巧。安德鲁·博斯沃斯（Boz）在他的个人网站boz.com上有很多关于如何进行评审的精彩文章——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm trying to get him on this podcast by the way.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我正努力邀请他来参加我的播客。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Oh, that sounds good. He's great.
turns.zh: 哦，听起来不错。他真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: He's great, he's fantastic. Let me know when you have him, I have some questions I want to get you to ask him. But Boz had a few ways of thinking. First of all, let's start with Zuck. Thing I loved about Zuck's exec reviews was that it was clear when you walked into the room that you are talking to one of the most powerful people on the planet. But what he did which not a lot of other people in this position do, is he would tell you what the rules of engagement were for every meeting or [inaudible 00:58:08]. He'd be like, "Look, I'm going to give you a spectrum of A, how much I care about this topic. Everything from I don't care, I don't know why you're talking to me, do I care kind of care little? I kind of care so I'm happy you're getting this update, do I really want you to do this? But you know what, if you overrule me, that's fine. All the way to I'm the founder, I'm the CEO, just do this." But he will make it clear where he stood on the spectrum. (00:58:27): The second thing he would make clear is why he believed the things he did. For example, the very first time I pitched him on what is the Facebook Audience Network which grew into probably one of the largest ad networks on mobile, he had all these sort of ideas, he was like, "We shouldn't do an ad network because," and he had all these opinions on, "Well, mobile ads all look terrible, they are spammy, X, Y and Z." But he was really good at articulating those to you and also saying, "Well, if you can prove me wrong on these legs of my logic tree, I will let you overrule me, unless I have a strong opinion." So when you walk in a meeting, you're like, "Well, I know the framework, I know what the dance is, do you convince him?" Or maybe there's no shot to convince him and that's fine. He's the CEO and that's fine too. (00:59:10): So I really learnt that it's so important to clarify for your team the framework you're operating in with you. And it's also maybe a clarifying function for yourself as so how do you actually feel about this and why do you feel like that? That's number one. The second part of it is inside a meeting, there's a few things I think you need to do which is clarify what kind of meeting is it. Is it just an update? "Great. We're just going to get an update? I'm going to listen to you, I'm going to applaud you for a job well done, I'm going to send you on your way." Or is it a decision in which case, what are the pros, cons, et cetera? There are some real big failure modes where one kind of meeting slides into another kind of meeting where somebody is like, "Why are we doing that? Is that a thing?" (00:59:46): And then somebody will start fighting on and people are like, "Oh gosh, we shouldn't have brought this topic at all." And everyone listening to this has probably been to one of those meetings. There's also something else which teams sometimes like to do, which is they'd be like, "Hey, we have a hard problem. We don't know what to do." They're trying to kind of push the responsibility of the [inaudible 01:00:02] from them to you which may be fine, but you should be like, "Hey, are you saying that you can't make up your mind and you want me to make up your mind for you?" You want to be very explicit because often I've seen this when there are hard decisions, teams are like, "The exec feels strongly, we don't want to know what to do," and they kind of want to push the accountability to you and here, we watch out for that a lot. (01:00:25): There are a lot of hygiene things we think are very important. For example, send out a pre-read before, make sure it's the right people in the room, not everybody, but not missing out key people. Make sure you're paying complete attention, make sure everyone gets a chance to talk which by the way, I was really bad at. And those things go a really long way. Oh, and one final thing, have a regular rhythm to those, so you're doing this every month, et cetera. What I hate, I stole this line from Gokul Rajaram, is the phrase, "Hero meetings." All of us have been this which is there's a big thing, there's a big review, it's probably a go/no-go, maybe it's career limiting, maybe it'll get our team funded and everyone is stressed out. You spent two weeks working on a deck and the first 20 minutes of conversation goes totally sideways because the exec thought of something. Every one of us has been one of those. Those are bad. (01:01:11): The way to fix that is to have a regular check in, so you have meeting every single week and becomes like you're not spending weeks, it a muscle, it's a rhythm of what you do and those are reason. Sorry, I went on a bit of a speech there.
turns.zh:
他太棒了，简直不可思议。等你招到他后，记得告诉我一声，我有几个问题想让他回答。不过博兹有几种思考方式。首先，让我们从扎克伯格说起。我最欣赏扎克伯格开会时的做法——当你走进会议室时，就能明显感觉到你正在与这个星球上最具影响力的人物对话。但他做了一件其他高管很少会做的事，那就是在每次会议前明确设定"交战规则"。他会说：“听着，我会给这个话题划分一个从‘我一点也不在乎’到‘我非常在乎’的等级。你们可能想知道我为什么要跟你们谈这个话题？我真的想让你们做这件事吗？但如果你们否决我的决定，那也没关系。直到最后一句：‘我才是创始人兼CEO，照办就是了。’”他会清晰地表明自己的立场。（00:58:27）  
第二点，他会解释自己为何持有某种观点。比如，我第一次向他推销Facebook的Audience Network（后来发展成移动广告领域最大的广告网络之一）时，他提出了各种质疑：“我们不应该做广告网络，因为……移动广告看起来很糟糕，充满垃圾信息，等等等等。” 但他善于清晰地传达这些观点，同时补充道：“如果你能反驳我逻辑树中的某个环节，我会让步，除非我坚信自己的判断。” 所以在会议开始时，你会清楚规则：是单纯汇报？还是需要决策？（00:59:10）  
最重要的是，要让团队明白你的决策框架。这也是自我反思的好机会：你对这个问题的看法是什么？为何持有这样的观点？第一步。第二步，在会议中，你需要明确会议类型。是单纯汇报？还是需要决策？如果是决策，就要分析利弊。很多时候，会议会从一种类型滑向另一种类型，比如有人质疑：“我们为什么要做这个？这有什么意义？”（00:59:46）  
还有团队常用的策略：他们会说：“我们遇到了难题，不知道该怎么办。” 试图把责任推给你。这没问题，但你得明确问：“你们是说自己拿不定主意，想让我替你们做决定吗？” 要保持清晰，因为在重大决策时，团队常会说：“高管意见很坚定，我们不需要决定”，然后把责任推给你。我们对此要格外警惕。（01:00:25）  
我们认为有很多细节很重要。比如，提前发送阅读材料，确保会议流程清晰。
会议中要确保关键人员到场，不一定人人到场，但不能遗漏关键人物。务必全神贯注，确保每个人都有发言机会——说实话，我在这方面做得很糟糕。这些细节至关重要。哦，最后一点，要保持会议的规律性，比如每月定期召开等。  
我特别讨厌（这句话借鉴了Gokul Rajaram的观点）“英雄会议”这个说法。我们都经历过这种情况：重大决策、关键评审，可能决定项目成败，或许影响个人职业发展，又或者是争取团队资金的时候。大家压力山大，花两周时间准备PPT，结果前20分钟的讨论因为高管临时想到新点子而偏离轨道。我们每个人都经历过这种糟糕的会议。  
解决之道在于建立定期沟通机制。比如每周固定开会，这样就不用花费数周时间准备材料了。这就像锻炼肌肉一样，形成固定的会议节奏，自然而然就能做好。抱歉，我刚才有点激动地说了太多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I was thinking about is you two have worked at basically all the big consumer companies and coming back to imposter syndrome briefly, what's the worst product you've built or the biggest failure you've each built and what did you learn?
turns.zh: 我想说的是，你们俩几乎在所有大型消费品公司都工作过。这里再简要谈谈冒充综合症（imposter syndrome），你们各自打造过最失败的产品或经历过最大的挫折，从中又获得了哪些教训？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Oh, man. At a startup, I tried all kinds of things. We kind of grasp at straws and build whatever. And also I think I fell victim to, a lot of startups do this where they'll see some theme that has become a meme with investors and they'll be like, "I'm going to go build that company. I'm just going to take that technology, adopt it." You're kind of start of seeing that with AI now where it's like everything is now an AI company. Of course everyone has incorporated AI part of it is you get it, you kind of want to be in the game and be cool, but if it doesn't really fit with your product hypothesis and thesis and what your customers are asking for, don't fall for that fad. (01:02:18): And I did stuff where I totally fell for the fad. I think I had a consumer electronics e-commerce, like a machine learning model where we rent and then recommend the right things to go buy. But then we were like, "Oh, Uber is doing this whole UberX thing where it was people having their cars and they could do this thing." And at that time, I think this whole shared ownership of stuff became such a big thing and I was like, "Oh, I'm going to do that exact thing where it's like it's less-
turns.zh: 天啊。在创业公司，我尝试过各种各样的东西。我们总是胡乱尝试，建建停停。我觉得自己也曾陷入很多创业公司的误区——比如看到某个主题在投资者中成为热门话题，就想：“我要去打造这样的公司，拿来那个技术，套用到我的产品上。”现在AI领域也出现这种情况，感觉所有公司都在做AI，但其实很多产品与客户需求并不契合。别盲目追随潮流。（01:02:18）我自己就曾深陷其中。我做过一个消费电子商务项目，用机器学习模型推荐用户购买商品，但当时Uber推出了UberX服务，让用户用自己的车接单。当时共享经济概念火热，我就想：“我也要做类似的业务，降低成本……”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 01:02:51].

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: At that time, we were partnering with Best Buy and we were like, "Well, we should do this other side product," which is people's own stuff that they could put up on the site. Total disaster because there is a lot totally different company logistics, everything. You could build it out as a different business, but we had a small team which was heavily focused on this business, was already doing pretty well and then we had to fork all of that effort to go build this other thing which required different skillset, different fulfillment technology and all of that. And so we were like, "Okay, disaster." So we pull the plug on it many months in, but we should have done it a lot sooner.
turns.zh: 当时我们正与百思买合作，觉得应该开发另一个副产品——让用户上传自己的商品。结果彻底失败，因为涉及完全不同的公司物流体系。原本团队专注于主业务，发展良好，但却要分散精力去开发需要不同技能、不同物流技术的新项目。几个月后我们不得不放弃，但其实应该更早停止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What you learn from that experience other than pulling the plug sooner?
turns.zh: 除了及时止损，还有什么教训？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah, don't fall for fads. It's do the thing that your customers are asking for and are willing to pay for. Or not even what your customers are asking for, but if you have something that is working, don't get distracted. It's very easy to be like, "I'm going to build this five other things and it's all going to accrue value." And I literally talked to another founder last week where they're like, "But I'm building this consumer thing, but I'm also going to do this SDK so I can go partner with these other companies and do this B2B thing." And I'm like, "But you are four people. Why are you doing that? That's crazy." "But imagine catering to 10X the market." I'm like, "Well, but you're going from a consumer payments thing to something like Stripe and that's a very different business, so do you want to go do that and go have that trade-off conversation?" So that was one big learning. At Netflix, we tried this out, we knew it was an experiment. This was before Netflix was cool like 10, 11 years ago, where [inaudible 01:04:27].
turns.zh: 是啊，别追逐潮流。专注于客户真正需要并愿意付费的产品。即便不完全符合客户需求，但只要现有产品有效，就别分心。创业者很容易想：“我要开发五个新项目，都能创造价值。” 上周我和另一位创始人聊，他说：“我要做这个消费者项目，同时开发SDK，合作B2B公司。” 我说：“但你们只有四个人。这太疯狂了。” 他说：“但我要覆盖10倍的市场。” 我说：“但你要从消费支付领域转向Stripe那样的B2B服务，完全是不同业务，你确定要这样做吗？” 这就是个深刻教训。在Netflix，我们尝试过类似实验，那时Netflix还没火，十多年前（[声音模糊]）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like DVD place?
turns.zh: 比如DVD租赁平台？

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah. So my job was to build the streaming player software that goes-
turns.zh: 是啊。所以我的工作就是开发流媒体播放器软件——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No big deal.
turns.zh: 没什么大不了的。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah. My job was to go partner with Samsung and Sony and Panasonic and build a software, the SDK that goes into TVs and set-top boxes and Blu-ray players. This is before international, Netflix and original content like House of Cards and all of that, but one of the experiments we tried back then was Netflix 3D. Total disaster [inaudible 01:04:57].

(01:06:53): In fact, the codename for Windows Mobile 5.0 was Crossbow and kind of a little secret which I think is kind of public now, Crossbow was a weed killer, it killed blackberries. (01:07:34): I learned two lessons from that. One is the market is bigger than all of you. turns.zh: 是啊。这是2005/2006年，所以就在iPhone问世前两年，当时我们刚毕业，两个年轻人一起参与了这个项目。当时基本上有个产品ID叫Visual Studio，还有个扩展功能，让你能在精简版的.NET Framework上写代码，然后在这些小手机和Pocket PC上运行应用程序。团队非常棒，我们至今还是朋友，如果没有那段经历，我们就不会有现在的工作和事业，所以这不是重点。重点是我们都知道那些手机速度慢、功能差，但当时总被告知：“听着，没人能改变现状，因为运营商控制着这个市场。他们决定手机和设备上能装什么软件，所以整个生态系统都在与黑莓竞争。”（01:06:53）：事实上，Windows Mobile 5.0的代号叫Crossbow，这个小秘密现在可能已经公开了。Crossbow是一种除草剂，能杀死黑莓。所以整个思路是如何攻占企业市场、对抗黑莓并与运营商合作？结果2007年，史蒂夫·乔布斯走上舞台说：“我有三个发布要宣布，实际上是一件事。”我记得给经理发短信说：“你一定要看这场发布会”，因为很明显这东西会改变一切。微软所有人都说：“不，运营商控制着一切，他们绝不会让这些设备上市[01:07:32]。”但事实证明并非如此。（01:07:34）：我从中吸取了两个教训。一是市场比你们所有人都大。你可以与优秀的团队、顶尖的公司合作，但如果市场转变，你无法克服糟糕的市场或糟糕的局面。第二点最关键，如果你觉得某个产品不好，觉得新事物更好用，你凭直觉就能感知到，就要顺从直觉。因为我记得当时想：“是啊，iPhone很酷，用起来顺手多了，但好吧，也许他们是对的，也许这——”

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: All these people are so much more senior than us, clearly they've put so much more thought into this, clearly what do I know kind of thing. And you realize that now, I think over, what, we've done product for 15, 16 years now, and we look at it and go, "We now have these patterns to go match against." We know when something is better, when something is working, when something feels like it's intuitive, you follow that intuition now then and not try and fight it and be like, "But here are all these things where this is not going to get there," kind of thing. It just doesn't work that way, the market ultimately wins.
turns.zh: 这些人都比我们资深得多，他们显然对此投入了更多心思。说实话，我又懂什么呢？现在回想起来，我们做产品已经15、16年了，再回头看，就会发现我们现在有了一套可以参照的模式。我们现在知道什么是更优的，什么是有效的，什么是符合直觉的。你只需要顺着这种直觉走，而不是固执己见，说：“但有些地方肯定行不通。”市场最终会证明一切。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: And I think when you're younger, you should really trust your instincts. And instincts can mean, "I just hear people talking about this other thing a lot," or, "I hear that other company's name come up a lot," or, "I tried this thing and... And you may not have the framework to articulate it and you may not trust your instincts, but there's something there and you should learn to listen to that voice. You're like, "Why is that? Why are we talking about it? Maybe they're doing better marketing, maybe their CEO is better on Twitter or they have Lenny Rachitsky as an angel investor or they advertise on your podcast," there we go. I tried to get a plug in there, Lenny. But you have to listen to your instinct because there's usually something there to follow.
turns.zh: 我觉得年轻的时候，你真的应该相信自己的直觉。直觉可能表现为：“我老是听到别人谈论别的东西”，或者“我老是听到别人提起另一家公司”，或者“我试过这个东西……” 你可能没有框架去清晰表达，也可能不相信自己的直觉，但那种感觉肯定存在。你会想：“为什么会这样？为什么大家都在谈论它？也许他们营销做得更好，或许他们的CEO更擅长玩推特，又或者他们有Lenny Rachitsky这样的天使投资人，或者他们在你的播客上投放广告了”，诸如此类。我本来想借机宣传一下Lenny的，但你必须倾听自己的直觉，因为通常那里确实有值得追随的东西。

turns.en: All right, I knew you were going to ask me this and I was thinking how do I be kind of balanced in-

turns.en: No, balanced and give measured answer and say, "Well, every framework has good and bad ways and there are good things and bad things," and I could probably given one of those answers. No, I actually think the more fun thing to do is I'm going to say I hate Jobs-to-be-Done, I think it's a terrible framework, I think no successful company has ever been built on top of JTBD and if you pick JTBD, you're probably doomed and here's why. Let's go back to the canonical example. And there's nothing Clayton Christensen who was a legend, amazing, the milkshake, what is the idea of being the milkshake? You are a person, you go into a commute and you're like, "Hey, I'm going to get this milkshake because it's the exact right quantity and save me on my commute." But they changed it up and all of a sudden, boom, it was not serving the job and look into the thing that actually it is serving the customer for. (01:10:39): I'll tell you that's not how actual real companies work because in real companies there are so many different parameters. For example, maybe it is really, really hard to go build that milkshake. Maybe there's another person who opens up across the street who builds a better milkshake than you do. Maybe the cup configuration in the car changes, maybe the supply chain for milkshake changes. But in my world, let me make this more concrete, when you work in social media, there are often so many other agents in the system where you can't focus on one person's equation. I'll give you an example. When you sign up for Instagram right now, when you sign up for Facebook for many, many years, Facebook knew that it needed to get you to 10 friends in 14 days. (01:11:14): If you got your 10 friends in 14 days, you were probably going to use Facebook. So it'd be like, "Well, we're going to throw every tool we have at our disposal to get you to 10 friends and 14 days." So if you signed up for Facebook for many, many years, you'll get this little thing called People You May Know. Then you'll have this person who just signed up for Facebook, you go, "Why I'm seeing this person?" It's not because you need a friend, because they need a friend. So what Facebook did was it made your experience slightly worse to make that person's experience slightly better. This was performing no job for you, it was trying to perform a job for them. Was the right trade-off or not? I don't know. We had this problem at Twitter. The single best product launched for the last five years at Twitter was the introduction of the algorithmic ranking and-
turns.zh: 别这样。给出一个平衡且谨慎的回答，比如：“嗯，每个框架都有优缺点，也有可取之处和不足之处。”但我可能更倾向于另一种说法。实际上，我觉得更有趣的做法是直言不讳：我讨厌“待办任务”（Jobs-to-be-Done）框架，认为它是个糟糕的框架，没有任何成功的公司是基于JTBD建立起来的，如果你选择JTBD，注定会失败。让我举个典型例子。克莱顿·克里斯滕森（Clayton Christensen）是位传奇人物，他的理论很棒，比如“奶昔”案例。奶昔的核心理念是什么？你是个普通人，通勤路上想：“我要买杯奶昔，因为它分量刚好能节省通勤时间。”但后来他们改了配方，奶昔突然不再满足用户需求。这才是真正企业运作的逻辑——现实中参数太多。比如，制作奶昔可能成本高昂，街边新开的店铺可能做得更好，杯子设计可能变更，供应链也可能调整。但现实中的社交媒体平台，比如Instagram和Facebook，多年来一直强制用户在14天内添加10个好友。成功后，用户会自然使用平台。但现在平台推出了“可能认识的人”功能，当你看到陌生人时，会疑惑：“为什么推荐这个人？”其实不是因为你需要朋友，而是平台需要用户添加好友。Facebook以牺牲你的体验为代价，提升了对方的体验。这是否值得？我不知道。推特也遇到过类似问题。过去五年推特推出的最佳产品是算法排序机制——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: God, hearsay. Oh my God.
turns.zh: 天哪，这都是道听途说。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: ... and it saved the company and power users hated it. They're like, "I know how to control my timeline, I know who to follow," et cetera, et cetera. It turns out though, this is not built for power users. It was really built for a regular person when they sign up for Twitter to be able to give them a great experience because we knew the power users, they already have. And by the way, TikTok really great example of that. So how do you make the trade-off? Do you pick power users or do you pick a regular person? What is the trade-off between them? Jobs-to-be-Done does not tell you that. (01:12:22): Let me tell you this. If you go order a package from Amazon right now, five years ago or three years ago, you would've gotten an email, it'll tell you what is that package, what is in it and when it's showing up doorstep. Last couple of years, it doesn't, why? Because Amazon doesn't want Google to have that data inside Gmail system. So it is, for very, very valid competitive reasons, made your experience worse because that's the right thing do for a company. So real life and real product is all about these trade-offs and whenever I've seen people trot out JTBD, it's a tell that they actually haven't dealt with a trade-off, where you have to make one person's life slightly worse in one situation for some other interesting dynamic. Okay, I'll stop with my mini speech [inaudible 01:13:02].
turns.zh: ……但这拯救了公司，而权力用户却讨厌它。他们会说：“我知道如何控制我的时间线，我知道该关注谁，”等等。然而事实证明，这个设计并非为权力用户打造的。它实际上是为普通用户设计的，当他们注册Twitter时，我们希望能为他们提供优质体验，因为我们知道权力用户已经有自己的控制方式了。顺便说一句，TikTok就是一个很好的例子。那么如何权衡利弊呢？是选择权力用户还是普通用户？它们之间的权衡是什么？Jobs-to-be-Done并不会告诉你这些。（01:12:22）让我告诉你，如果你现在在亚马逊上下单，和五年前或三年前相比，你会收到一封邮件，告知你包裹内容以及预计送达时间。但最近几年却不再这样了，为什么呢？因为亚马逊不想让谷歌在Gmail系统中获取这些数据。所以出于非常合理的竞争原因，他们让你的体验变差了，因为这对公司来说是正确的选择。现实生活和产品设计中到处都是这样的权衡。每当我看到有人拿Jobs-to-be-Done说事时，往往意味着他们从未真正面对过权衡——即在某种情况下让某个人的生活稍微变糟，以换取其他有趣的动态。好吧，我就不继续我的小演讲了[01:13:02不可听清]。

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah, I think JTPD, the problem with that is it's just too idealistic. And most frameworks are, but this one just takes it up a notch where it's like it's almost meant for people who are so naive about product building and especially product building at scale. I think it might work for the V1 or just a hypothesis that you're trying to go test out, where it's like, "What is the core value that we are trying to serve for this user," kind of thing. But really V2, V3, it kind of falls apart because you have these super hard trade-offs that you have to make and every company goes through that. So it's almost a little too idealistic in its thinking. I think that's the biggest problem with it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得Jobs-to-be-Done的问题在于它太理想化了。大多数框架都是如此，但这个框架更甚——它几乎是为那些对产品开发，尤其是大规模产品开发过于天真的人设计的。我认为它可能适用于V1版本，或者只是你试图测试的假设，比如“我们要为这个用户提供什么核心价值”之类的。但到了V2或V3阶段，它就开始崩塌了，因为你必须做出极其艰难的权衡，每个公司都会经历这个过程。所以它的思维方式有点过于理想化了。我认为这是它最大的问题。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, and look, I was being a bit bombastic obviously and it does have some [inaudible 01:13:48].
turns.zh: 是啊，看，我显然有点夸张了，这里面确实有些[01:13:48不可听清]。

turns.zh: 我们会把这部分剪掉。这是[01:13:49不可听清]。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Yeah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. It's may be useful in some niche case which nobody has ever heard about-
turns.zh: 是啊，啦啦啦啦啦啦啦啦。这可能在某个没人听说过的小众案例中有用——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: For milkshakes.
turns.zh: 比如奶昔。

turns.speaker: Sriram Krishnan
turns.en: Right, for milkshakes. Yeah, if you're starting a milkshake company, go for it. But I'll say, so people have good [inaudible 01:14:01] what is the alternate, would involve not JTBD, how do we actually figure this out? And I think a much better way and I really understand the early Facebook years, which is systems thinking. Think of all the players in the system, think of all of their incentives and how they interact with each other. So in that milkshake example, your car, the person, the competitor across the road, the supply chain, the profit margin of each person, the podcast they have to listen to, what is each person's incentives that you're trying to drive and look at how they all work together. (01:14:31): So for example, so then when you look at the algorithmic rankings case, sure it kind of deprioritized a certain set of people, but it prioritized the other set of people and you could then have a much more rational discussion about whether that trade-off is worth it. Maybe it is, maybe it's not, but it's a much better discussion that, "Well, that person wanted milkshake, we're not giving them milkshake," what do you do? That doesn't help you at all. And yes, it may be a good tool in ways that I absolutely have not seen so far, but-
turns.zh: 好的，关于奶昔的。是啊，如果你要创办一家奶昔公司，那就放手去做吧。但我要说的是，让人们真正理解用户需求（JTBD）并非易事。我们该如何具体破解这个难题呢？我认为一个更好的方法——我深有体会的是Facebook早期的系统思维——是把系统中的所有参与者都考虑进去，了解他们的动机以及彼此之间的互动方式。以奶昔案例为例，涉及你的车、顾客、对面竞争对手、供应链、各方的利润率，还有他们必须收听的播客。关键在于，你要清楚每个参与者的动机，并观察他们如何协同运作。（01:14:31）比如说，在算法排名案例中，系统确实降低了某些用户的优先级，但同时提升了另一组用户的优先级。这时候你就能更理性地讨论这种权衡是否值得了。或许值得，或许不值得，但这样的讨论比简单地说“某人想要奶昔，我们却不给他们奶昔”要有意义得多。这根本无济于事。当然，或许它在某些方面确实是个好工具，但——

turns.speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
turns.en: Yeah, also the other tool I think I really like is first principles thinking. Everyone throws it out there, it's kind of become this cliche now, but really think about it as if your product didn't exist and if you had to start over from scratch, would you build it the exact same way for these set of customers?
